PLEASANT SURPRISE. —My dear," said young Mr. Marage," what is this dessert, anyway ? " 'lt's called surprise pudding," replied the dear young thing. "I tried to bake bread, but it wouldn't rise, so I just made a nice wine sauce for it and made it do for dessert."

"Now that I have promised to be yours for ever and ever," she said, as she looked up into his eyes, "tell me, Harold, if I am the only girl you ever loved." " Ah, nly darling," he replied, "can you not content yourself with ,the assurance that you are the only girl who ever loved me?" "Come here, Johnny! I'm going to give you a piece of " " Oh, mamma, is it apple pie or custard?" "How dare you interrupt me, Johnny ! Come here; I'm going to give you a piece of advice." MAMMA : "Well, Johnny, I shall forgive you this time, and it's very pretty of you to write a letter and say your's sorry." Johnny: "Yes, ma; don't tear it up, please." Mamma: Why not? Johnny: "Because it will do next time." MAGISTRATE: "You are charged with running over an old lady while scorching. What have you to say in 'regard to this awful accident?" Defen- dant: "Awful accident? Why, a little thing like that doesn't hurt a good bicycle like mine is! " WIFE : "I'm going to run across the street just a minute to bid Mrs. Jones good-bye." Husband: "Well, you'll have to hurry; the train leaves in three hours."

Didn't even give me a ebonce to say to my friends that I'd be lucky if I ever got it back ! ' A CAREFUL WOMAN.—" Speaking of women with saving dispositions," said Dixmyth, "m wife's in a class all by herself." "How so? queried his friend Hojax. "Last week I bought an upright piano," replied Dixmyth, "and my wife made a beautiful green plush cover for it, se the polish wouldn't get scratched. Yesterday she made another cover of linen to go over the plush to prevent that from getting soiled. Next week I suppose she'll make a calico cover to protect the linen. Oh, I tell you women have great, big, fertile minds." "DARING," said the young man, as he tenderly raised the lovely head from the place where it had rested an hour or more, got up, sat down again on the other side of the beautiful maiden, and once

more drew the golden curls to his bosom, "you have no objection to this slight change of position, have you ? " "No, Alfred, she murmured softly, your heart is on this side." "Yes, my angel, ' responded the young man, his voice trembling with deep feeling, "and my vest will now get worn alike on both sides." "WE'LL have to give up the idea of puttin pictures in the parlour, Jane," remarked Old John Turnipseed, as he threw the bridle under the table. "Why ?" asked his wife. "Too dear! Why, I priced one in town to-day, and the dealer sez, sez he: That's an old master; its price is £500.' " Why,' sez I, it looks like a secondhand pictur.' " 'Ys it is,' sez he. "Then, thinks I, if a second hand pictur costs that much, it's no use to price a new un. So, Jane, I reckon we'll have to hang up a few mottoes, and the like, and let the pictur s go."

NEAT COAT AND SKIRT.

rapidly from one extreme to the other. Our country relations will, no doubt, rejoice to hear that short skirts are becoming fashionable even in the great centres of fashion. Of course a long trained skirt is impossible and most uncomfortable wear in the country, and only a woman devoid of all good taste would think of setting out for a walk across the fields thus burdened, The shirt instead should be cut to clear the ground perfectly all round while it is not so abreviated as a cycling skirt. Some of those people who are devoted to the long skirt have hit upon a cunning device for converting it into a short one. This is done by providing a shaped volant which is attached underneath the upper volant which constitutes the skirt proper, by means of buttons and buttonholes. By attaching the second volant to the skirt increased length is given while the general aspect is of a double flounced skirt, such as is at present so fashionable. My second h illustrates the skirt I have just described,
Of course for afternoon wear or indoors the long skirt is undoubtedly vastly more graceful and adds height to a short figure.

for early autumn weir there are some very charming colours, most of which are old friends in a newer and bettqr guise. Grey, which was so popular all last season, is not so much in favour, and there is a decided leaning towards green and warm russet tints, while petunia and violet are also much in vogue. These are seen at their best in tweeds and honre,pons, both of which are good wearing materials and can stand all sorts and conditions of weather. Many of us, however, will have to make our last season's clothes do duty for another yfar, and if these ware properly brushed and repaired before folding them away, it is wonderful how fresh they will emerge from their seclusion. It will be found well worth the expense entailed to send a coat and skirt to the cleaners or better still to pot it in.the hands of a tailor to have it thoroughly cleaned and hot pressed. A small jobbing tailcr will do this quite as effectually and probably cheaper than the large firms. However well meaning our attempts it is impossible for a prentice hand to get the lines of the coat seams properly into shilpe. An old coat looks wonderfully smarter for the addition of a leather collar and strapping,s. If, however, we have to do the best we can ourselves, expense being a matter of such great importance that we cannot afford the necessary five or six we must use a damp cloth and iron the wrong side of the material. Grease stains can be removed from all 'woollen materials by spreading the garment on 'a table and rubbing some powdered borax into the spots with the fingers. Let it stay for a few minutes and then brush the borax off with a clean brush. -

A smart autumn hat is depicted. It is of bright navy blue strafiv trimmed with a twist of green velvet and scfme wings, whose colours gleam in blue and green. This combination of blue and green is quite the smartest thing in
HAT.

the world of millinery just now, and is becoming to Most people. The feathers must be set at an almost impertinent angle, as the effect of the hat depends on their arrangement. A thin blue gauze veil may be worn with a hat of this description for travelling or when out in stormy weather, as it will protect a delicate skiu. For those who wish to freshen up their last year's coloured straw hat the followiag hints will be found useful. First brush thoroughly, then dissolve a piece of gum arabic about the size of a nut in three tablespoonfuls of cold water. Brush the hat well with this solution, being careful the brush goes into every crevice and hang the hat up till dry, keeping it in the shade.

div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Visitors to the State Apartments at Windsor Castle aTe now charged for admission, the proceeds being devoted to local charities. At first sfght the turning of Windsor Castle into a show place at pnpular prices seems a little incongruous, but nu one will object to the charge of Is for adults, and 6d for children, more especially as the gementa for chewing the rooms have been greatly improved.

Until recently the vomit were all covered up when the Castle was open to the public,and they generally had the appearance of being prepared for redecoration. Now the furniture can be seen without its holland covers,and the rooms are ahewn almost as they are lived in. V. hen their Majesties are away. the Castle is usually open to the public on Tuesdays, Wednesdays,and Thursdays,but it is best to select a fine bright day for a visit ; as the light in most of the reams is none too geod,and scarcely does justice to the pictures, which alone are well worth seeing. The Kinglis not a very ardent sportsman with the'gun, and foe in any seasons he has usually been either at Homburg or Marienbad at this time of the year. As a rule it was not until after the Doncaster race meeting, that his Majesty went to Scotland for deer driving whion he prefers to grouse or partridge shooting. There is, in fact, very little of the latter at Balmoral, where the grouse have been chiefly preserved for the royal table. The deer forests on the other band, offer excellent sport, the forests of Abergeldie and White:mouth being filled with game, and great pains have been taken to improve the deer on the Balmoral estates, where the forests ex- tend right to Birkhall, and to the edge of the moors. There is, to the clean, water-loving individual, some- thing peculiarly uninviting in the thought of the "mud bath" se frequently recommended by doctors now-a- days. We have, however had plenty of time in which to get accustomed to the idea,for it has had the sanction of science for many generations. Speaking generally, a "mud bath" is composed of peaty boggy turf, which contains stimulating chemical properties, and which being carefully prepared, is mixed with the mineral waters of the locality where it is used. For the com- fort of intending bathers, it may be mentioned that the mixture is not adhesive, but leaves the skin easily under the warm douche which precedes the cleansing bath. Those of us who have not yet cultivated the habit of sleeping with our bedroom windowa open should com- mence this very excellent practice without delay, when it will be possible to go through the winter with at least an inch or so open at the top at night. Many a head- ache and heavy feeling could be avoided by following thishailemare being taken of course that the bed is placeci out of the draught. Those people subject to neuralgia or sold in the head, should arrange a curtain so as to avoid all chance of taking a chill and persevere with this open window plan, which ironer or later must prove beneficial to them. A woman who can afford but one winter tailor-made coat and skirt, would do well to select a smooth cloth, wherewith to have this built, and black she should re- member is under such circumstances much to be pre- ferred. lewdness of this dlscription is invariably be- coming and smart ; It does not date so quickly as whoa built of a colour; it is never out of place, and it make, the figure look slender. Then the possibilities in the way of colour schemes are practically andlese. Vests and stocks can be of any tint preferred, the shade in every case being carefully repeated in the bat and underskirt, of course. _

. - In skirts we are promised three distinct styles. For walking there will be the abort pleated variety, osten- sibly made to clear the ground, but which will need just as much careful bolding up as the trailing skirt, and is really more difficult to manage. Then there will be the fuller, longer, and much trimmed skirt for indoor and outdoor afternoon wear, and last of all the very long, sweeping, and elaborate evening skirt. In coats eccen- tricities seem to be the order of the day, but unless one is able to closely fellow Dame Fashion's whims, it is better far to avoie these, and remain faithful to the neat little semi-fitting varieties, that just cover the hips, and can be warn open or closed. Fur pelerines, with the cape deeply pointed at the hies and stole ends which reach almost to thefeet in front, have quite taken the place of the round fur boas, and are much more sensible and desirable in every way. They protect the lungs, and leave the throat unmufflei, and moreover impart a very smart appearance to the wearer.. ..By the way, the tendency in this winters furs Is not to mix different skins, but to make clever mani- pulations of one kind, which is also a move in the right direction. The effect of an attempt to blend together three or four different kinds of fur, too often suggeetyl a dip into the oddment bag, and frequently made for the ridiculous.

Nowhere has the movement for the equality of t e sexes made such progress as in Australasia, and a further illustration of this is afforded by a case, reported in the Melbourne papers In which a woman was sum- moned to show cause why she should not centribute to the eunport of her husband. If such proceedings become genoral,it would afford another argument for the reform of the marriage service as, despite the assumption in the Prayer Book, it was decided that the wife was liable. She was well to do, whilst her husband was a State pensioner, and she was ordered to pay so much par week for her husbands maintenance.

Few religious orders do more useful work than the organisation known as the Little Sisters of the roor,wh with noticing patience collect what money they receive by appeals from door to door. By these means they are able to maintain a large number of old and helpless people in their houses, of which there are something like 25 or 30 in the .United Kingdom, the Order was originally founded at St. Baryon in Brittany in 1840. but it has since spread all over the world, and it is said the Little Sisters are instrumental in ?providing be- tween forty and fifty thousand old people with a com- fortable home for their declining years. --
MADGE•

Brighton has the reputation of containing the oldest subject of the Biog. His name is Charles Green. He is 108 years of age ; he still retains all his faculties, has a clear recollection of the days of George 111., and can enjoy a good meal. Green,who was born in Bussex,and was for some years a licensed victualler in Brighton, re- sidPs with his son at a little hostelry known locally as "The Hole in the Wall," situate near the West Pier. Be welcomes visitors in the bar parlour, and will chat pleasantly with sympathising friends Be has been a non-smoker all his life.

div.head: PART 11.—CHAPTER 11. (continued.)
div.p: PART 11.—CHAPTER 11. (continued.)

Before the morning everybody in Dipford had heard of Joseph Lamb's luck. Folk talked about tt in the inn, on the road,, and in the farm kitchens. For weeks no one spoke af anything but Joseph's Legacy. When he.went to chapel on the following Sunday, the eyes of the congregation were upon him, and, blushing self-consciously, he led Naomi to a pew. When the plate was passed round at the end of the sermon, Joseph drew a handful of silver from his pocket, and presented a shilling towards defraying the travelling expenses of the visiting minister from Exeter. A few days before Whitsuntide, Tozer granted the lad a half-holiday to go to Newton. Jingling Len sovereigns in his pocket, Joseph sauntered up the street, looking into the shop windows, with an s.cute itching to spend money. His wants had ncreased marvellously during the past month, for he seemed to possess an almost unlimited purchas- ing power; and when one has wealth it is difficult to know how to employ one's money. In a tailor's window he saw some handsome and genteel suits, the very late:,t articles in tweed, of a horsey, showy pattern and cut. Joseph entered the shop. "Suit, sir ? yes, sir," said the polite shopman. "To measure, or ready made." "One of them in the winder," replied Joseph. "Those are grand value; only two guineas complete," said the man. "Just try on the coat, sir. Ah, fits you like a glove Grand cloth this; wears like wood." Before Joseph left the shop, he had parted with three of his sovereigns for a loud check suit, two white shirts, a pair of merino pants, two pairs of socks, a gaudy striped necktie, and a white, round felt hat.

At a pawnbroker's he bought an enormous second-hand silver watch, sold at the great sacrifice of twenty-six shillings, and warranted to keep time. Then he purchased a pair of heavy ...to for working-days, and a lighter pair for Sundays, with pointed toes and kid uppers. A resplendent display of dresses in a draper's shop made him think of Naomi. He meant to buy her a present. What could be more useful than a dress?"

He went inside and asked for a lady's dress. The two girls behind the counter turned aside to giggle as the shop-walker led Joseph to the costume department. "A dress for a lady ? " said the assistant, smiling. "What age might the lady be?" " My age," said Joseph. "About fourteen or fifteen? How do you like these mixtures, wool and silk? We're selling these at two guineas-amts.-half, and they're very sty- lish. You would like something pretty, wouldn't you?, Joseph rubbed his head as he passed from one dress-stand to another in the long room. "I reckon these are all too big," he said. "They could easily be made to fit. Here's a lovely thing!" returned the young lady, pointing to a 'bright lilac costume. "I'd best have that one," said Joseph. "I shan't never decide if I look at all these others. It's a pretty dress." "Do you think that one will do? It's for your sister, I suppose ?" "No, ma'am, it's not for my sister. I ain't got one," replied Joseph, flushing a deep red through his sunburnt skin. " Ah, a sweetheart, then," said the assistant. "Pin sure she'll be delighted. I'll put it in a box for you." It was dark when Joseph came into the kitchen at Smerdon Barton carrying two huge parcels and three smaller packages. " Lord-a-mercy I what has the boy been buyin' ?" I said Mrs. Tozer. "Have you spent all your money? I knew it would burn a hole in your ; breeches pocket." "rye spent 'most all," said Joseph. "What in the workl have you got in that draper's box?" asked Farmer Tozer. "A dress for Naomi, sir," said the boy. "I suppose ehe's to bed." " Yea, and seinen for an hour, I reckon," said Mrs. Tozer. "Well to be sure! 'Twas good- natured o' you to think of Naomi." After the dross had been admired by the farmer and his wife, Joseph carried his purchases to his room; and when he had spread the things on the bed, he went along the passage, and knocked at Naomi's doer.
"Be you usl6ep, Naomi !" he asked. "Who's there? Is it Joe?" came a muffled voice.

" Yes ; I've bought you a beautiful laylock dress. Can't you conie and see it?" "Oh, Joe—u, really ! Bide a minute, while I slip on my pettico.A ; then you can come in." Joseph returned lor the dress, and hanging it over his arm, he waited in the passage. • "Now I'm ntedy," said Naomi, presently, open- ing the door, ,n,l smiling bashfully as she stood in deshabille, Ulth her tawny hair descending upon her nightgown, and her little white legs showing beneath her petticaat. "There !" sail Joseph, holding the dress before her glowing foe.. "Oh, Joe, ! a real gentlefolks' dress ! " she cried. "It must 'a' cost a sight o' money, sure enough !" "So it di]," cmill Joseph. "I must try it, on right to once," she exclaimed, excitedly. "o,'a go out till I call'e Joe, and then you sh9l ?PO how smart I look." Joseph is itioirew. In a few minutes Naomi re- opened the door, and appeared in the gorgeous costume. ' -
" Isn't it ?" she said. saA Joe. "I hardly know you in it, Naomi. Won't folk stare at the chapel?" "There ain't a grander dress in Dipforcl, I'll bo bound

"No, I don't think there is," said Joseph. "It don't quite vit. e'Tis too long in the bodice, and the skirt tirag ; but I can get Miss Carson to alter it. Thli•i; ..o;t, Joe; you're very good." • She came up to ii,n and put her lips to his cheek. " Now run away," she said. "It's time we was both tp sleep."

div.head: CHAPTER 111.
div.p: CHAPTER 111.

Dipford feist is an ancient merrymaking insti- tuted in Tudor times, and still held yearly just before the busy s.iuPLin of corn harvesting. At this revel you may se he best wrestlers of the West, competing for the fat hog and the barrel of cider presented by the Lord of the Manor; and the swiftest runners ;racing for a silver cup. It is a day of frolic, junketing, jigging, and kissing the jolliest day et the year. The church bells begin to peal blithely at ten in he morning; the Dipford Band brays the " Old English Gentleman " and "The Roast Beef of Old England," while the villagers and folk from far and near troop to the Vicarage.field, where booths are stacked wit 4 hogs- heads of ale and cider, and a ring of closely mown turf is roped off for the " wrastlers." All the hinds at Smerdon Barton had leave to attend the feast ;,and for a week before the great day, you heard Flrmer Tozer and his men discuss- ing-the prowess cf Jan Cann, the famous wrestler of Middlecomlie village; and the fleetness of young Nick Dicker, of BrS,dhembury, who had travelled as far as Taui,!o:C to run against the pick of the Somerset athletes, " Is it goen to be vine on Monday?" was the question continually asl:ed. by Naomi. " How can us tell?" replied Dick Truscott, "I wouldn't ine no reckonin' on vine weather. It depends on the Powers above." On the Sat urilay, Farmer Tozer tapped the baro- meter, and liek his head. "Looks all like wet for the Yeast," MI said, at dinner time. "Glass has gone back, 'most to much rain." . _ _

In the evening rain-clouds drifted over the Clatter-rocks, veiling the grim pinnacles; and Joseph and Naomi watched the leaden sky from the stable window, with anxious faces. "Oh, Jce, 'tis goen to be wet on Monday, I'm vire 'tis'," said Naomi, dolefully. It looks all like it," was Joseph's pessimistic rejoiner. "God can make it vine if He's a mind," said gaomi. "Let's pray, Joe." "1 dunno how to make good prayers out loud," Joseph said, as they knelt down on the cobble stones.
"We must both zay : Please God send vine weather on Monday. Nevertheless, Thy will be lone. Amen."
------ --- They repeated the invocation aloud, while Shot, the spaniel, watched them with his head inclined Dn one side, and his stumpy flag slowly sweeping the floor.

The sun rose m ernrison and purple on Monday; -.ix' though Naomi remembered the shepheliffe well known augury of a red sky in the morning,. as she sat upright in bed to watch the dawn, the clouds packed and fled when the sun was high above the black whale-shaped Haldon Hills. At nine Naomi finished her morning's work, and went upstairs to put on the lilac dress. Miss Carson, the village dressmaker, had shaped the costume to the girl's dumpy figure, and its splendour and modish ways of trimming and cut had been the talk of all the young women in the parish. "Well, if you don't take the shine off zome of the maid's dresses, my name ain't what it is !" exclaimed Farmer Tozer. _ . . . .

- When Naomi came down, Joseph was clad in his new check suit and white hat, with a showy, white-spotted blue necktie, and a full-blown pink cabbage rose in his button-hole. His hair was well oiled, and his cheeks shone with, yellow soap. The sports began at eleven, and by that time the Vicarage field was bright with the dresses of the girls, the fluttering of flags on the booths, and at the bowling alleys set up by gipsies. Joseph and Kaomi staid close up to the rope of the wrestling ling, amid a bevy of lasses who were chattering and laughing. Euphemia Smith, the daughter of the landlord of'the Artichoke, at Middlecombe, was the leading spirit of this group; and whenever she made a sarcastic comment upon NaomPs resplendent dress all the girls laughed merrily. The idea of her wearin' laylock with red hair I" said Euphemia. " Carrotty's the colour," giggled Clara Joyce. "I don't care how much ;he was to spend on clothes, she'd never look , genteel," continued Euphemia. "Her figure puts me in mind of a loose zack of oats, tied in the middle. I vi ender she did hut have a green parasol, and a scarlet feather in her hat. Look at her gloves I They 'm a zize too. big; and no one wears white cotton gloves now." Naom, drew nearer to Joseph. She kitew that she had incurred the feminine jealousy of the village; that, but for Joseph, she stood unfriended among her neighbours. A tear dropped ti ein her lower lid, and rolled down her freckled citek ; but she smiled when her sweetheart whispered: ••llen't mind them, Naomi. They're very spiteful, and it's all becos you look so nice." "I've heard that them laylock dresses is quite out o' vashion," said Euphemia. "You don't zee none o' the gentlevolk in 'ern. A lady's got more taste." But cheers drowned Enpheinia's ba'..easuns. as the famous Jan Cann and Wtil Petherwit), of, Dip- ford, stood up for the first bout. When the wrestling and running matchPs had been decided, the dancing courl,.seAttel;:i: the ring, and the band struck up a polka. Tree young farmers were refused by Euphemia, who selected a smart young man from Exeter as her partner for the first dance.
"Would you like to dance?" said Joseph to Naomi. I'm afeaied that., I can't do much at it, 'cos Tye never learned it."

" No ; they'll only laugh at us," replied Naomi. She was smarting from the sting of Euphemia's gibes, and she no longer wished to be a conspicuous object in the crowd. The criticisms upon her dress had set her thinking upon the contrast between her short, plump figure and the lithe grace of Euphemia. Such a shape as Euphemia's would look charming in almost any kind of costume.
'She's right; I don't look at all nice—only silly," was NaomPs reflection, while she watched the dancers. _ _

After the polka, Euphemia's face was flushed and radiant with smiles as she rejoined her com- panions. "Don't you dance ? " she said to Joseph, with one of her most entrancing pouts. The boy glanced shyly at this handsome, fully. developed maiden, with the large brown eyes and the clear pink skin. He was angry with her for sneering at Naomi, but yet he felt himself honoured when she deigned to speak to him. "I don't know how, he answered. "Oh, a polka's easy enough," said Euphemia. "I could get you through all right. Will you dance with me next time?"

The kindness of the request, and her emphasis as she said " me," quite disarmed the simple lad. He knew that by consenting he would wound Naomi; but the temptation of arousing the envy of the three farmers and the young gentleman from Exeter was too powerful to be resisted. Undoubtedly, Euphemia was the prettiest girl and the best dancer in the field. It was generous and condescending to ask him to dance with her. His heart fluttered and his cheeks flushed.

"Do try," she said, in a soft, coaxing voice. "Very well," he answered with a shy snigger. " That's right," said Euphercia. Without a word to Naomi, Joseph led his partner into the ring. He was conscious of a hundred eyes fixed upon him as he stood by her. Presently, the music began; and Joseph, taking his cue from the other dancers, put his arm around Euphemia's slim waist, and found himself footing it clumsily in and out of the throng. "Why, you're gettiii' on capitally!" said Eupliemia. "You'd zoon learn. Do you like it ? " Her smiling face was close to his, so close that he could see every vein, and feel her breath upon his cheek. "Yes," he said.

_ The polka ended with a flourish from the musicians, and Joseph looked round for Nvmi. But she had left the dancing ring; he could na see the bright lilac dress in the crowd. Euphemia kept close to his side.

"Do you ever come to Micldlecombe ?" she asked. . "Sometimes I pass through with the cart, when • I go to fetch coal." "Mind you call in and have a glass of mother's sloe gin," said Eirphemia. "I shall be glad to see you. "Thank you," he said, glowing with flattered vanity. "Are you lookin' fot the young girl from Smerdon 7' asked Eupliemia. "Poor thing! I believe you've made her jealous, clancin' with me." "I expect she's somewhere about," said Joseph; but just then he had no 'desire to leave his pretty new acquaintance. Euphemia. Smith was seventeen, but in astuteness and worldly wisdom she Was far older than her years. She had boasted to Clara Joyce that she could " hook " any fellow..; mut for purely merce- nary motives she had determined to try her arts upon the un.ophisticated ,Joseph Lirnb. There was little doubt in her mind that he would be an easy victim, for everyone knew that he was " soft " and silly-minded. She had no romantic notions about love. What she wanted was a weak, docile husband, with enough money to start in business as a publican in Newton. Her parents were of the money-making species, and she had inherited their acquisitiveness, and imbibed their shrewd counsels. For the unsuspecting Joseph, the day of the feast proved a turning-point. His susceptible heart was won by the amiable condescensions of this hand- some, stylishly-dressed girl; and in a sort of inebriation of pleasure and pride he walked by her side to the refreshment booth, where he paid for her luncheon. Several times during the afternoon, he thought of Naomi, and wondered where she was; but, with only a slight sense of self-reproach, he realised that Euphemia was far more attractive than the little red-haired, freckled maid at the farm. '
At eight o'clock Joseph returnea alone to the farm. Mrs. Tozer was having her iupper in the kitchen.

"Well, you'm a pretty chap to go sweetheart. in'," she said. "Here's poor Naomi been home zince three o'clock, and wi' eyes quite red wi' cryin'. _I asked her what was to do, and she zays as you vorsook her to dance wi' that flash young gal o' Smith's, to Middlecombe. A nice giddy zort o' head you'm got on your shoulders !" Joseph ate his bread-and-cheese in silence' feel- ing that he had acted ill towards Naomi. When he went upstairs, he listened outside Naomi's door; but hearing no sound, he crept back to his bed- room, and was soon snoring in the bright August moonlight that lit every corner of the little room. It was light when Naomi awoke, and the first object that caught her eye was the lilac dress hanging on a peg. All the glory seemed to have fled from it since yesterday morning. She almost tutted the sight of it. For the first time she was alive to the ruthless cruelty of the fates; and in a re-access of disappointment and disillusionment, the tears flowed to her eyes, and wetted the pillow on which she had sobbed herself to sleep. When Joseph left her, without a word or a glance, t 4 dance with the publican's showy daughter, Naomi's heart was like a leaden weight, and a hard lump grew in her throat. The sneers at her finery were like stabs; and when Joseph parted from her, she felt the keenest humiliation as she stofxl among Euphemia's giggling companions. During the time that she roamed disconsolately in the crowd at the feast, she lost all interest in the games and the fun. The laughter and the music mocked at her and saddened her; and suffering the bitterness of an unfulfilled, long-cherished_expectation of a corn.

pretely happy trilumpriant dayTehe went from the field to weep-alene. When the hinds sat down to breakfast, Joseph was ashamed to look Naomi in the face. Her eye- lids were swollen, and everyone could see that shc had been crying that morning. But the talk was of the splendid bout between Jan Cann and young Will Petherwin, the running, and the jumping; and Naomi was relieved frozq the dread of being questioned. She had carefully folded the lilac dress, and put it in a drawer, covering it with newspaper, and laying a piece of camphor in the folds, to keep away the moths. Such beautiful vesture was not for poor maids, with plain faces it only made them appear ridiculous. And in time, when the wound of Joseph's faithlessness had healed, she bravely accepted the inevitableness of her limitations in the way of beauty, and found content in homely print and linsey, while she treasured the lilac costume for the few happy memories it had yielded her. It is one of our compensations that callow love, sweet though it be, never takes complete sway of our hearts. In these first flights of passion we are most of us foredoomed to endure the pain of unre- quited love; but the world before us is full of new experiences and illusions, and in youth time is not slow to heal hurts of the body or mind. A grief which to Naomi seemed inconsolable, resolved itself in the course of a month into the opinion that the transference of the inconstant Joseph's affec- tien we not a matter for secret sorrow ; and, theugli jealousy tinged her childish philosophy, she neeer upbraided her errant swain. Euphemia Smith found her admirer as plastic as dough ;indeed, he was so easily moulded to her wishes that the process lost much of the interest and excitement which would have accompanied the entire subjuation of a high-spirited lover. At her direction, Joseph gave up farm work for the less robust employment of serving in a public-house bar at Newton, in order that he might learn the busi- ness by the time that he was entitled to the £B5O. It cannot be said that Fumblefist possessed even an average share of those qualities that make for individuality of character; but such independence as he had, was soon annihilated when he became the humble knight of the imperious Euphemia. He married at the age of eighteen-and-a-half, and at nineteen he began a career as innkeeper, or, to be strictly precise in the use of terms, barman and cellarman of an inn under the control of his wife. Far two years he drudged in patience, never once resenting, the withering taunts of the woman wile despised him. He had always held that he was born to sorrow, and despite the inheritance of the £B5O he maintained that opinion; for the money 'brought no permanent satisfaction, but the reverse.
One day Fumblefist walked into the kitchen at Smerdon Barton, as though he was still a member of the household, and, with a deep sigh, he said tc Tozer:

_ "I hear you're wantin' a man. I've come tc offer myself, and I wish Pa never left you. Last Tuesday my wife went off with a man from Torquay, and I ain't sorry, neither. I've sold the public, and I'll be glad to come back to Smerdon." And so Joseph Lamb became hind again tc Farmer Tozer, at a wage of five shillings a week and his board.
THE END.
A WISE SCHOOLBOY.

Ten-years-old George Chambers, the son of a well- known Dublin veterinary surgeon, asked at school to construct a sentence in which the word " cure" appear- ed, promptly wrote "Bile Beans cure Biliousness. As proof of the wide recognition of this imporrant fact, it may be stated that the master accepted the sentence as a perfectly matter-of-fact one, just as if the boy had written "Nature's remedies are the safest cure for Nature's ills." Bile Beane are purely vegetable, and in all oases of biliousness and liver disorder ate unequtlled. All chemists stook them at one and three-halfpence and two and nine per box. Mrs E Simsnonds of Parfett-street, Commercial-road, London, E., says :—" After the birth of my first child I frequently suffered from bilious attacks, together with constipation and piles. Some- times my food, however carefully selected, would return, and for days at a stretch I was AO bihoul as to be practically useless in the house. Until I tried Bil Beans nothing seemed to touch my complaint. In Bile Beans, however, I found a remedy ; and after fourteen long years ill-health they have quite restored me. As a mark of gratitude I shall always recommend them." Here is powerful corroboration of the truth contained in the school-sentence. If yes suffer note it well.

div.head: REVISING THE VOTERS' LISTS. Court at Warrington.
div.p: REVISING THE VOTERS' LISTS. Court at Warrington.

The proceedings at the opening of the revision court at the Warrington Town Hall on Monday, by Mr James Foard, barrister, were of &purely formal character, - and occupied only thirty minutes. Mr John Clayton represented the Liberals, and Mr William Holbrook the Conservative& Mr W B Woodcock, assistant overseer and assistant borough treasurer, and Messrs T J Garnett and F H Aukland (relieving officers of the union) wero ,also present. The Corporation were represented by Mr Stanley Wilson, the deputy town clerk. The lists contain 11,327 names—an increase of 20a on last year's number: The number of claims was 216, as against 221 last year, and the objections 102, as against 14/. The total claims and objections last year numbered 368, which was 3'2 per ,cent on the list. This year the num- ber was 318, :Witch was 28 per cent. There were 12 lodger claims, and 25 reclaims by lodgers.

div.head: SOLICITOR'S CLAIM.
div.p: A SOLICITOR'S CLAIM.

_ Anether Sitting of the Court was held on Monday evening. Fred George Taylor, solicitor, claimed a lodger vote in respect at rooms at 274, Idanchestererosd. Mr Woodcock stated that the value of the house was £25 gross. In answer to Mr Clayton, cirimant said he occupied a-bedroom on the first flocr and a sitting room on the ground floor, furnished. Be bad the exclusive use of the bedroom. If be required the (xeusive use of the sitting room for study or business he was absolutely entitled to it. He would not go so far as to say that he would exclude everyone from the room. The rest of tbe family had the use of it very often. Mr Clayton : Have you the exclusive use of the sitting-room P

Applicant: I can have it every day of the year if I like. I don't live apart from my family for the sake of getting a vote. The Barrister : I am afraid the description is in- correct. You have the absolute use of the bedroom,but I am afraid you have only a joint use of the sitting- room. The claim is bad. The proper form in which to claim is for a bedroom on the first floor exclusively and as a joint user of the other room. It is only a con- d;tional occupation. Further questioned by Mr Clayton,claimant said there were eight or nine rooms in the house. The Barrister: I will amend the second claim and put in user of the sitting7roorn. - -

Mr Clayton : This is " a case of a son." Considering the number of rooms in the house the claimant can scarcely get the necessary value. He cannot get his £lO. There is insufficient value in the bedroom.

The Barrister : It is a nice peint, certainly. Mr Clayton : And he admits the sitting-room is not for his exclusive use. Claimant : I don't say anything of the kind. I can have the room whenever I went it.
The Barrister : I don't think you can attach any im- portance to that. Perhaps the other side may say "No, you can: ot exclude us. We have a right to have our meals there."
Claimant: If you raise the print I shall ask you to adjourn the further hearing of ttuf case. \ _

'lle Barrister: The only matter to consider is the value of the bedroom. I should have felt inclined to allow the claim myself, but if Mr Clayton objects I can- not do so. I don't think there is £lO in the bedroom. It must be worth £lO unfurnished. Mr Clayton : Even if you take the two rooms I don't think youlcon get the va'u, on the £25 gross. The Barrister: lam afraid I cannot allow the vote There is not a good case so fares the £lO is concerned. Mr Clayton : That is the point. The Barrister: Raise the point to-morrow morning and I will look into the matter in the meantime.

"A BEGGARLY ARRAY OF EMPTY BENCHES." The reAston was continued on Tuesday morning, but the business occupied a few minutes only, and was of a purely formal charac'er. There was only one claimant. The Barrister : Is that all P Mr Holbrook lam afraid it is, sir. The Barrister : What a brggarly array of empty beocbes.! .(Laughter).
SCIr Woodcock said the present revision established a record so far as the number of claimants was concerned
Mr FAard attended on Wednesday tor the putpose signing the lists and " starring duplicates."

In the course of an inquest at Cardiff upon a girl who was burnt to death in a thoroughfare close to Liandaff Cathedral it was stated that most of the members of a crowd which collected showed indifference to bee suffer- ings and refused the help that might have saved her life. VAC an inquest in Devonshire on Tuesday it was stated that the wife of a gipsv who had cut his throat ran to ao, farmhouse for help. The farmer ret lied to her appeal by the statement that he had to" milk his COW 3 and go to church," and advised her to proceed to the next farm. Elie indifference was condemned severely by the coroner and the foreman of the Jury.

div.p: NEWS ITEMS.

The death occurred on Saturday at the age of 86 of Mr. Philip James Bailey, of Nottingham. He is best known by his poem " Fes:us " which was published in 1839. One of the most beautiful passage! in this work tuns as follows We live in deeds, not years ; in thoughts, net breaths ; In feelings, not in figures on a dial. We should count time by heart-throbs. He most lives Who thinks most, feels the noblest, acts the best. And he whose heart beats quickest lives the longest : Lives in one hour more than in velars do some Whose fat blood sleeps as it slips along their veins.

Madame Patti and Mr John Santley visited Brecon last week, and sang at a concert, both artists giving their services in aid of the County and Borough In fir- Mary. The concert was well patronised, and the eminent artiste and Mr Santley had a hearty recall on rendering the duet" La Ci Darem," from Don Giovanni. They returned and commenced the opening passages of the piece when it was notic,cl that the singers appeared to be in some unusual difficulty. Mr Santlev at length ceased singing, Madame Patti continued for a bar or two, and then both convulsed with laughs,er left the stage. Some of the audience in the front seats who had noticed the cause of discomfiture joined in the outburst, and then, in response to continued plaudits. ht'i &elates returned, and Madame Patti explained that a wasp had been paying her and Mr Santlev such persistent atten- tion that they found it difficult to proceed with the encore. The unwelcome intruder had tried to enter her mouth, and at last they had had to beat a retreat.

At the Liverpool Po'ice Curt, on Monday, John Ben- sit, jun., was summoned at the instance of the Asaist- ant Head Constab'e for having uttered language likely to occasion a breach of the peace, and to show cause why he should not consent to find sureties for his future good b.thaviour. Police evidence was given as to the disturbances which arose at the meetings addressed by the defen- dant. Some lively passages-at-arms between the sti- lpendiary magistrate and the defendant's solicitor ensued and finally the defendant elected to go to gaol rather than find sureties for his good behaviour. Mr Stewart accordingly passed sentence 04 three months' imprisonment, and the defendant loudlr pro- claiming that so long as God gave him breath he would continue to preach the Gospel and expose error, was taken into custody. Two men, who had been guilty of creating a disturbance at one of Mr Kersit's meetings, were each ordered to find one surety to be of good be- haviour for twelve months, or go to prison for fourteen days. In each case the surety was forthcoming.

A remarkable accident, and one that affects the safety of Blackpool as a bathing ground. occurred at Blackpool On Saturday morning. About 600 yards from the Pro_ rnenade, and a little to the south of the Victoria Pier there is a channel in which has collected a quantity of mud and slay, part of which had drifted from the ex-, eavations for the Promenade extension works. Following a custom she practised at the seaside, Mrs Elizabeth Underwood,, aged 51, of 16, Mowbray-street, Infirmary-square, Leicester, left ,her lodgings about 7.30 to wade in the sea. About 8.10 an aetsndant at the Victoria Pier heard that a woman was drowning and on rushing to the spot he found Mrs Underwood lying dead, face downwards, in two feet of water. The Unfortunate lady was the mother of one of the Black- pool police constables, and several mernbra of the force were soon on the scene.—lt was found that the body Was so securely fixed in the mud that it was impossible to tsmove it without ropes. These were obtained from the Victoria Pier, and a number of men and women helped the police drag the body out. The operation was not anattended with danger, for Police-constable Foster ot stuck in the mud and sank to his waist, and the rescue party had to direct their labours towards getting him out, which was done after considerable difficulty. Ides Underwood, who came down to Blackpool with one other dauahters on September Ist, was to have returned home on Saturday,

Captain Hudson, who Must have seen the cliffs from the bridge of the egiapnad the same time as ourselves, for immediately he called to the engineer to go astern full speed. The order was very quickly obeyed. Just before we began to go astern the keel of the vessel was felt touching the rooks ; but it was so slight that she did not cugtain the slightest injury. There was great excitement for a minute or two, and cries from some of the lady passengers till they were assured that there was no real danger. We backed out a considerable distance, and still going very slow groped our way to Douglas." On reaching that port half an hour later the Calais Douvres -narrowly escaped collision with the Empress Queen, which was 'backing out from the pier OD her return to Liverpool. The sides of the two vessels almost touched each other, There were 700 people aboard the Calais Douvres, and among them wigs Mr gigginbottom, M.P., one of the proprie- tors. Great credit is due to the engineer and captain for their able handling of the ship, for they just averted a disaster. The passengers (said our informant) expressed towards them both high praise, and this was cordially endorsed by Mr Higginbottom himself. All the steamers were delayed by the fog, which cleared in the evening, but was at times during the afternoon as dense as has been seen for yearg off the Manx Coast. Several large orders, amounting in the aggregstl to hundred of thousands of tons of coal, have just been Placed with South Lancash're colliery firms for shipment to various ports in the United Rats. The continued disastrous strike of miners in Pennsylvania is causing agents to come over to this country, in order to niece entr acts. The Lancashire coal trade is showing signs f I improvement, fuller time being now worked at 50 e cent the collieries in Southern Lancashire, corn- ed with a month ago.

div.head: EDUCATION BILL. Letter from A. H. Crosfield.
div.p: THE EDUCATION BILL. Letter from A. H. Crosfield.
[TO THE EDITOR OF THE 4' EXAMINER:]

Dear Sir,—A short time since you were good enough to print a powerful and important letter in the Education question by Mr Roundell with a few comments thereon which I ventured to send you. May I now again ask you to draw your readers' attantion to the pithy and pregnant letter from Dr Macnamara which appeared in the "Man- chester Guardian " last w-ek. The letter may be left to speak for itself and like Mr Roundell's is I think well worth the attention of anyone who takes the:least interes,, in this alkimportant ques- tion. Yours faithfully _

div.head: September 2nri 1902.
div.p: September 2nri 1902.
Dr F J Haciaatuara' ecter reads as follows :

It is quite clear that the defeat or the with- drawal of the ilducation Bill is a contiagency with ['which we must now reckon. This being so I would venture to ask all those who care for our country's future to consider where we stand in this vital 'matter of the equipment of to-morrow's citizens. Roughly, half the working-class children of the country are in attendance at Board schools ; half at Voluntary Schools. The financial support accor- ded to these schools is of two kinds—central and local. The central support consists of grants from the Exchequer paid upon the reports of The Majesty's inspectors of schools. Generally speaking, tnese grants aYe paid both to Board and to Voluntary schools upon pretty much the same terms, but are admit- tedly not sufficient of themselves to meet the cost of conducting the school with efficiency. To cover the deficiency there must be a local contribution.ln the case of the Board schools this is supplied from the public rates; in the case of the Voluntary schools recourse must be had to the pockets of voluntary contributors, many of whom are already paying the local school board rate. Tons, be it observed, we seek to maintain the education of at least half the working-class children of the country in part at the hand of charity. Let the friend of national progress note the re- sult. Twenty-eight shillings and twopence was the local public contribution from toe rates last lyear in respect of each Board school chill. 6s 8d the corresponding local private contribution in re- spect of each Voluntary school child. Broadly, then, each Voluntary school child receives an education crippled by a financial disability of from 15s to 203 out of a total maintenance expenditure of some 60s per year. To those who are not altogether blinded by sectarian rancour this is the really acute educa- tion problem of the moment. See what it involves. In the Board schools 53 per cent of the teachers engaged are fully qualified adult teachers, the others being partially or wholly unqualified young persons and juveniles ; in the volnntary schools only 39 per cent. of the teachers are certificated adults. In the Board schools there is a certificated teacher for every 74 of the children enrolled ; in the voluntary schools a certi- ficated teacher for every 103 of the children enrolled Apply the touchstone of comparison at any point and you get the same alarming result—a result which must be most disquieting to anyone who realises that the proper education of the child now in the Voluntary school is precisely as important a national affair as the education of the child now in the Board school. Now what is it that this Bill, with all its manifold faults, , essays to do? It seeks to sweep away once and for all the dangerous anachronism ' of endeavouring to equip the children by voluntary contributions. It seeks to throw these voluntary schools boldly upon the rates for their local sus- tenance. (Personally I would rather see education entirely or almost entirely maintained as a " national " service by the exchequer, but at any rate I am vehemently against a continuance of the voluntary contribution fiasco). And why cannot this urgent reform be accomplished ? Partly be- cause of sectarian rancour; but partly,also, because the Government has not been ready to accept frankly the concomitant to its policy of rate aid for the denominational schools. That concomitant Is obviously full and complete public control ; and no matter how carefully it may be hedged around by all sorts of expedients, it is bound to come. Dr Temple saw that clearly enough when he urged denominationalists not to put their schools upon "the slippery slope of the rates." In their wisdom they have deliberately decided to do so. But it is futile to seek to evade the consequences. indeed if Mr Balfour's gerrymandering scheme of two-sixths representation for the public upon the local management of the denominational schools were passed into law to-morrow how long would it last? I would give it ten years at the outside—ten , years of acute local bickerings, at the end of which time we should be on the highway to a thoroughly national system of public elementary education. In the meantime will the Government take note of the signs of the times and concede a larger measure of public control? If not, will its bill be beaten? And if so, what then? Will the Unionist policy be that of another small Exchequer dole for those starving Voluntary schools? Will the Liberal policy be that of allowing the Voluntary schools slowly and painfully to be squeezed out of exist- ence by competition with the Board schools? And are these latter schools to continue in their now truncated and cockertonised condition, ruled down to the merest rudiments and giving education in practically the three It's only to children under 15, and deprived of any right to conduct evening schools ?

These are, as it seems to me, questions which call for immediate answer. It is not enough, as I ven- ture to think, for progressive educationists to con- fine their efforts to the endeavour to kill the pre- sent Bill. They must be ready with an effective alternative ; the alternative of (a) public education co-ordinated in all its grades; (b) public elemen- tary education maintained exclusively from public sources mainly, if not entirely nationally ; and (e) public education administered in each area of suit- able size by effective local boards of education directly responsible to the people of the locality. The Rev. F. E. Powell and Undenominationalism.

Writing to the " Manchester Guardian," the Rev Francis E Powell, of St James'a Vicarage, Warrington, says :—As one who has closely followed the progress— is it retrogression ?—of the Education Bill, and the criticisms to which it is obviously open, may I be allowed one more word on the " moral monstrosity " of undenominationalism ? It is just this, which does not deter you from criticising the bill, which compels us keenly te criticise it, for still maintaining the unwork- able and irritating compromise of 1870. In theory it is no doubt possible to recognize " a great measure of common truth which underlies all differences of expres sion," but in practice men usually approach religious truth as it expresses itself in certain well-defined , religious formularies or communities to whittle they are severally attached. Theoretically one is glad to believe and to know that there is much, very much, in common between the Jew, the Roman, the Unitarian, the Churchman, and the Protestant Nonconformist. But, after all, that which has made these what they are is not what is common to them all, but that which differentiates them one from another. Your argument for the undenominational ideal in State schools wculd hold good if you could persuade men that the specific is as nothing compared to the generic. But many fear that with the elimination of the specific interest the generic would wane. " That rather middling bishop but very eminent knave " Talleyrand knew well how to explain the absolute failure of an eclectic religion com- pounded of all that was best, truest, and noblest in all the faiths of the world. We knew, too, how Professor Huxley (Life, vol. ii., p. 339) Jought to " make a cento out of the works" of what he called the Naztreniapa of Jesus. prophetic Judaism, the best Stoics, Spinoza and Goethe. " There," he said, "is a religion for men." But although again and again he essayed to "do for theology what he had done for zoology," he never accomplished his design, and little good would have re- sulted from it if lie had. It is not thus that religions which will inspire, illumine, and comfort are made. i And even fit were possible so to manufacture Such " moral monsters" as the Eclectic Religion submitlisd to Talleyrand, Huxley's cent° or " religion for men," or School Board undenominationalism,why' we still demand to know, should the adherents of these religions, or those who assert their contentment with them, he the only ones paid for out of rates and taxes gathered from all sorts and conditions of. men ? Moreover, if there is anything inspiring, 1119imnating,and comforting in "on- denominationalism," is it net b i ecause those Noncon- formists who welcome t see in it an apnroximation— more ov less close—to much of the Nonconformist i teaching of to-day ? And f this be tr, it is manifestly unfair to those who do not accept this teaching that it and it alone—although with a perfectly amazing incon- sistency such allow Judaism to be taught in State schools without protest—should be established by the , State and endowed out of the rates. By all means let ; those who like School Board religioa have it, but, in the acred name of religious liberty, do not let the Jews be i he cnly others whe are tolerated n State schools.

HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT. Dr. SEPHTON presented reports upon the health of the district during the months ending August 13-,h and September 10th respectively. During the first-named period there were 27 births and 13th deaths. The death rate was equal to 144 per 1,000 against 277 the average of the last three months, and 16.06 for the correspond- ing month last year. Thirteen deaths occurred in the Asylums at Winwick and the death rate exclusive of these was 7 7 per 1,000. During the second month there were 24 births and 19 deaths. The death rate was 21 per 1,000 against 25.4 for the last three months and 13.2 for the corresponding month of last year. Toirteen deaths occured in the Asylum and the death rate exclu• Islam of these was 6•6 per 1,000. The reports were adopted. div.head: AN OBJECTOR TO VACCINATION.
div.p: AN OBJECTOR TO VACCINATION.

Pock-Marked Faces in Warrington. tha Warrington Pollee Court on Tuesday, Joseph Lowe Elaine-street, applied for a certificate exempting his cisild from vscoinstion. The magistrates on the Bette] were A'dermen Sutton (presiding) and Shaw Green and Dr Fox. _ _ _ .

_.„ Applicant stated that he believed vaccinatlon would be detrimental to the health of the child. The Chairman. On what grounds? Applicant: I think the putting of foul matter into any child would be detrimental. The Chairman said that according to applicant's ideas he knew more about vaccination than all the medical practitioners in the cpuntry. He was entitled to his opinion but they had found tram experience that it was those who bad not been vaccinated who suffered the most from small-pox. I Applicant said he had had two ther children vaccin- ated, but it did not "take " with one of them ; and I that child had been far healthier tl.an the other. He had also seen in the " Examiner " that, according to the report of the Royal Commission of Vaccination res- pecting the epidemic of small-nex at Warrington in 1892-3, although 99.2 per cent of the inhabitants had been vaccinated, there were more pock-marked faces in Warrington than anywhere else in Europe.

- Dr Fox : That •g not erne. The Chairman said he had not seen anyone marked with swill-pox in Warrington for years. Dr Fox told the applicant that he had a duty to the State and to his fellow-subjects in protecting them from sonall-poz. The application was granted.

..,.. The Leeds and Liverpool Canal Company. The balance-sheet of the Leeds and Liverpool Canal Company for the past six months discloses no improvement on he corresponding period •ef 1901. The receipts were slightly less, being £78,031, against £78.250.a decline of £2l9,while the expendi- ture was .£1,240 m0re—£62,326, against £61,086 in the first half of 1901. The cost ot the Investigation ICommittee, however, accounted for .£370 of this amount. The net result was that £15,705 was carried to net revenue account, against £17.164 a year ago. Debenture interest and other prior charges require £8,279, against £5,042, and the £2,500 specially set aside for repairs reduces the divisible balance to £8,288, a decrease on last year of £2,320. Twelve months ago it was decided not , to pay any dividend on the Ordinary Stock in view lof the drought then existing, and after paving the •1 dividend on the Preference Stock £8,623 was carried over. Again the Ordinary dividend will be passed, but the sum carried forward is reduced to Z 8,288.
RUN :OVER BY AN ENGINE. -- A Warrington Porter's Sad Death.

An inquest was conducted at Warrington on Saturday I by Mr S Brighouse, county coroner, touching the death of Thomas Beckett, a passenger porter in the employ of the Cheshire Lines Committee, residing at 6, Tineley's - terrace, who died at the Infirmary on the previous Thursday from the effects of injuries sustained by being knocked down and run over by a light engine. Mr Crompton (Messrs Browne and Crompton), appeared for the relatives of the deceased, and Mr Simpson repre- sented the C.L.C. Councillor Wilcock was foreman of the jury. The Coroner informe I the jury that on the previous Monday deceased was acting as shunter, and was en- gaged in dividing special trains in number three siding, about two hundred yards from the east end of the plat- form. Deceased had attached the engine to the South- port carriages and signalled to the driver to go on the main line. It was suppond that he then stepped out of the six-foot into the four-foot and a light engine which was coming into the aiding ran over him. In answer to the Coroner, Mr Simpson said deceased had been employed on the rail way about twelve years, and the company very much regretted his loss. He was s very cempetent man. Elizabeth Beekett, deceased's widow, gave evidence and said deceased was 32 years of age. Nurse Holroyd said deceased was admitted to the Infirmary at 9 o'clock on Monday evening suffering from fractured ribs, fractured left leg, and three scalp wounds, and died at 3.30 on Thursday afternoon. Henry Barlow, an engine driver in the employ of the Great Central Railway Company, said he arrived at Central Station on Monday evening in charge of a light engine from Manchester. The engine proceeded to the siding in larder to take a train from Warrington to Man- chester. When the engine got to the end of the train which was being divided witnese heard a moan, and on getting out of tee engine found deceased had been run ever. George Marshall, foreman passenger shunter, said the deeeased was a passenger porter, but on the Ddenday night in question he wasengaged as • passenger shunter, assisting witness. The deceased had done similar work to that in which he was engaged on the Monday for six months. He understood it perfectly. In answer to the Coroner, witness said that the traffic was congested on the night in que3tion. If it had not been, the light engine would hove gone down the main line instead of proceeding to the siding. The Coroner said that accounted for the accident. A verdict of " Accidental death " was returned, no blame being attached to anyone.

Cycling Accidents at Warrington. about noon on Saturday, a Newton fitter named James Taylor was cycling over Warrington Bridge when his wheel skidded and he fell on the road. A spring cart which was passing ran over his foot and injured his great toe. P.C. Corbett, who was on point duty,rendered first aid,and Taylor was afterwards driven tome. The event was a Pure accident.—At 3.45 on Tuesday afternoon,Philip HanlOw, an officer servant's at Orforn Barracks,was cycling out of Fennel-street into Criurch-et. when he collided with the horses attached to a 'bus which was being driven by Daniel Roberts. He was, of course, thrown to the ground, and the wheels of the 'bus passed over the machine,completely wreck- ing it. Fortunately the cyclist escaped unhurt.

div.head: New Nesleyan Ministers for Warrington.
div.p: The New Nesleyan Ministers for Warrington.

On Sunday the recently appointed ministers of the Warrington Wesleyan circuit, the Rev G H Careson (superintendent) and the Rev R W Rees, preached their first sermons in Bold-street and Bewsey-road churches. At the first-named place of worship the pulpit was occupied in the morning Mr Rees and in doe evening by Mr Carnson. At Bewsey-road Church Mr Carnson preached in the morning and Mr Reed in the evening. Nine years ago Mr Carnson was invited to Bewsey-road to take charge of the church there, but at the Wesleyan Conference the Rev Owen Watkins, a returned foreign missionary, was appointed,, and Mr Carnsen took up duties elsewhere —At Bold-street church there was a large congregation. Before the sermon, the choir rendered Gounod's "Send out thy light" in a creditable manner. Mr F Hickman presiding at the organ. The preacher took for his text, the words " Forbearing one another," and drew atten- tion to many of the present-day evils which would he averted were a spirit of gentleness and forbearance to become manifest among the people of the world. With regard to forbearance in parents Mr Rees said that in parental duty to-day there was a deprrssing amount of Musses to children in many grades of society. How many children had their lives made a burden to them by repeated (threats of punishment, by increasing repti- mends, and a lamentable leek of forbearance P—ln the afternoon the superintendent minister,Rev G II Carnson visited Bold-street Sunday School and addressed the scholars. Ia the evening he preached his first sermon at Bold-streets Church. The congregation was exceed- ingly large, and the singing was a special feature of the service. The rev gentleman preached from the words " Return unto thy house and show bow great thing God has done." He preaohed upon Chriatiani,.y as related to the needs of modern life. The anthem " 0 Lord, how manifold are Thy works " (Baroby) was efficiently rendered by the choir, Mr Frank Hickman again presid- ing at the organ. Mee Booth gave an excellent render- ing of the sole " 0 Divine Redeemer" (Gounod). The service concluded with the Vesper Hymn.

div.head: Christ Church, Latchford.—The Bishop of Chester Dedicates the New Aisle.
div.p: Christ Church, Latchford.—The Bishop of Chester Dedicates the New Aisle.

A large congregation assembled in Christ Church. Latchford, on Saturday afternoon,when the Lord Bishop of Chester (the Right Rev. Dr. Jayne) dedicated the new north aisle. The object of the extension has been to Increase the accommodation, and this has been obtained by erecting on the north side of the:nave theahale measur hag 591 t 6in in length and having a width from the nave of 17 feet. The north wal I f the nave has been replaced by a stone arcade, and the wall itself rebuilt on the outside of the new aisle. The north and west aisle win- dows are also the old ones removed from the nave. The gain in accommodation is about 95 Beatings. The heat- ing and the lighing of the church have been re-arranged and augmented. The decoration of the church end extensions has not eels had attention. The total expen- diture will be about £1,300. The work has been carried out by Mr Harry Fairclough, contractor, with the following local nab-contractors :—Stonework, Mr E Aukland ; plastering, Messrs Osborne and Sons ; plumb- ing, Mr Hughes. The whole of the work has been carried out from the designs of Messrs William and Segar Owen. The clergy present at the service were the Revs F A Sereeton (vicar of Christ Church), Richard Greenall (rector of Grappenhall aid patron of the living of Christ Church) ; E C E Carleton, F E Powell, and H V Pigot. Evensong (shortened) having been gone through, the Bishop dedicated the new aisle, making use of the fol- lowing weria : "In the faith aif Jesus Christ and la the name of His Church and people we dedicate this addition to this church to the honour and glery of God, the Father, Son and Holy Spirit." The sermon was preached by the Bishop from the words :—" Be ye also enlarged " 11. Corinthians vi. part of the 13th verse.— The preacher said it was a tempting thing to go back to early Vines because, as everyone knew, Latchford had an ancient history. Its ford was of great importance in the Roman times, certainly before the Roman Conquest, lard it was bound up with a great deal of interesting history. Leaving that subject on one side, he would refer to the history of that little church, which bad grown into such a large one. It was their privileze to have with them that afternoon the Rector of Grappen- hall the patron of the living,whose voice they had heard, the faithful pastor who was in charge of the church before it had actually become a separate church. In 1861 the church was built and was consecrated as a memorial to Mr Thomas Greenall. In 1873 an enlarge- ment took place very largely aided by the then Vicar, Mr Wade Powell, whose memory ought not to have altogether paged away. Fle was the brother of one who was still with them—the most faithful,stauch and liberal layman of the church. Although he was very unostenta- tious he contributed largely himself towards the sum required for the extension of the church and also did something towares the extension of the National schools and the endowment of the living. There had been a very considerable growth in the population of the neigh- bourhood. The Ship Canal had caused and was con- tinually causing new buildings to be erected, and the extension of Warrington was contributing to the same result, and, therefore, quite obviously there was a need for the enlargement of that church. The most graeify- ing thing of all was that the need for the extension came from the neighbourhood, and the demand had been met 'in a very prompt, thorough and liberal manner. £1.200 had been spent upon the enlargement and £2OO had been raised out of the parish itself in sums ranging from 23 8d to £lOO. And how welcome were the smaller sums. The incumbent and churchwardens wished to see the work of the church, " bread based " in the sympathy and interest of the people, and he hoped they would all find that the enlargement was a great conven- ience, and encourage those who had hitherto felt that there was little room for them in the church, and in- duce them to come more frequently. The inadequate stipend of the ministt‘r had been increased, and there had also been a substantial increase in the work of the church itself. Charles Kinsley had put these words into the mouth of one of his heroes in " West ward Ho ! " " The true reward of having done good work is to have more to do." That was the only reward they ought to look forward to on earth—the power and the opportun- ity to do better and higher service. The offertories at this service, the services held en Sunday, and others yet to be held, are to be given to the enlargement fund, for which a further sum of £135 is needed.

Onoe more the County Championship is over, and once more (one might almost write "as usual ") Yorkshire has triumphed in the great cricket contest, which always excites such interest throughout the country. The season just past has been a great contrast to its immediate predecessors, and the constant tale of rain and bad weather have told considerably in favour of the bowlers, who have proved that the batsmen are not so entirely their masters as was asserted during the recent dry summers. So in a way, though greatly inter- rupted and broken up, there has been a good deal of interest in these other aspects of the game, while the contest for the County Championship, which is little, if at all, affected by a visit from the Australians. has excited as keen competition as ever. It was almost a foregone conclusion that Yorkshire would head the list, but it could hardly have been anticipated that the Tykes would equal their grand record of last year, and only suffer one defeat in their twenty-five inter-county games. That, without detracting from the performance of Somerset, ever the county of surprises, must be admitted to have been somewhat of a fluke on a tricky wicket, when both teams scored very low, and the Westerners managed to win by a few runs. But thirteen wins, one loss and eleven draws must be accounted a great record, especially as most, if not quite all, of the drawn games were due to rain and were in Yorkshire's favour. Lord Hawke has captained his team as ably as ever, if not quite as frequently, and he has been most splendidly backed by Mr. F. S. Jackson, who after two years out of first-class cricket, has returned better than ever. As an all - round man he is only equalled by Hirst, and two such fine cricketers are a splendid nucleus for any team. Mr. T. L. Taylor, who heads the averages with 45, is a fine bat and an excellent wicket-keeper, and thus also doubly worth his place in the team, Of Rhodes and Haigh, whose bowling analyses are simply marvellous, it may truly be said that they too if only they were allowed, would undoubtedly too, splendid batsmen, and their form, when facing opposition bowling, is now anything but inconsiderable. Sussex' despite Mr, C. B. Fry having been out of form and Ranjit- sinjhi only having assisted intermittently, is a very good second, thanks to Tate's bowling and their general consistency of form : and so steady has been their improvement that even without their two crack bats they can turn out a very level and strong eleven. Since its first foundation as the "Commissariat and Transport Staff," the Army Service Corps has always been most unjustly lookedf down upon with that snobbishness so common in the service and so much deprecated by the truest and best soldiers; and it may be said that it has usually come in for more kicks than ha'pence and more hard
H. 8.8. FIELD-MARSHAL THE DUKE- OF CONNAUGHT, E.G.
THE EMT COLONEL4N-CHIRF OF THE ARMY SERVWE CORPS.

work than thanks on all hands. However, deqpite these discOuragements, official and otherwise, it has always continued to do its duty doggedly and efficiently; and during the receut %war, when Led with an almost herculean task, it carried out its work as well as, if not better than, any other branch of the service: and without the A.S.C. victory in South Africa would have been little short of impossible. Therefore, it was with a feeling of genuine pleasure that the announcement in the Gazette was read that 11.11.11. Field-Marshal the the Duke of Connaught had been appointed Colonel- in-Chief of the Corps. Hitherto it had lacked this ornamental distinction, which belong" to every other regiment and section of the Army; but now they can boast that few, if any, have such a distinguished Colonel-in-Chief as they possess in the King's popular soldier brother. His selection for the post is intended as a mark of esteem of the services of the Army Service Corps at the front, and the appointment of an officer of such rank and standing is greatly appreciated by the -if thr • itself. In its present state it has only been in existence for some fourteen years, and it may be said to have won its spurs very rapidly. In future the Army will feel that it is a branch to be proud of, not to belittle. Next week Lieutenant- General Sir John Prench takes up

the command of LIEUTENANT the First Army-GLNERAL SIB JOHN Corps at Alder- shotFßENCH, to which he Iwuo TARES UP THE ("034MAND OF was appointed TUE FIRST ARMY CfIRPS AT ALDS:R- SHOT ON bEPTl,llll:rin 153:11. upon the retire- ment of General Sir Redvers. Buller. At the time, however, he was doing too good service in South Africa to be spared: and -Sir Henry- Hildyard took over the command as a locitm tenens, until such time as General French was free to turn his attention to the quieter side of Army routine. Aldershot is very keen about its new commander, and a public reception is being organised in his honour.
Considerable interest has been excited by the decision of the Commander-in-Chief and the War Oafs te accept the proposal put forward by Mo.,

div.head: ilt. MARK MAYHEW
div.p: ilt. MARK MAYHEW
FOUNDER OF THE AUTOMOBILE VOLUNTEIM cortrt.

provide a driver for it. This will be strictly con- fined to the limits of the United Kingdom, and in time of peace will consist of driving staff officers during manuceuvres and on tours of inspection. No one will be called out for more than a fortnight at a time for the former or five days for the latter purpose, while members will be suitably paid for their services by the War Office, ann provided with a uniform, which has been designed by Mr. Mayhew and is khaki in colour. A certain number of officers will be appointed, but all members, whatever their rank, will be treated as volunteers and gentlemen. All damages incurred will be compensated for; and motor-cycles will be welcomed for despatch work. Mr. Mayhew hopes to enrol at least a hundred members, in time to commence serious work next summer; and already a good number of well-known automobilists have joined, including Messrs. C. S. Rolls, Du Oros, Letts, Cordingly, Crampton, Owers, Bird, and others. Many others are expected to join as the result of Mr. Mayhew's circular, especially as the terms of service are so much more attractive than those usually offered to volunteers, and no out-of- pocket expenses will be incurred on what should prove a pleasant little holiday from time to time. Of course, apart from this corps, there will be a certain number of official motor-cars in regular employ, as the experiments made by the Duke of Connaught, Lord Roberts, Sir Evelyn Wood. Sir Henry Trotter and others, have proved the value of the automobile for staff work. The new corps should be a success and very useful for Army purposes, and it is hoped that Mr. Mayhew will meet with support on all sides, civil as well as military.

A prince in the bankruptcy court is not an everyday occurrence, but Prince Victor Dhnleep Singh is unfortunate enough to find himself in this paradoxical position. For many years he has lived at Rockwood Hall, near Brandon, in Norfolk, where his shooting-parties, as well as his other forms of entertainment, have been notable. His popularity in society has been very great since his days at Eton and subsequent service in the Royal Dragoons. la 1898 he married Lady Anne Coventry, daughter of the Earl of Coventry, and this alliance went far to cement his position as an lEnglishman to all intents and purposes. Ha was born in England and Queen Victoria was his god-mother, and in every way he was brought up as an English country gentle- man. As every- body knows, be- hind his peculiar position of an Oriental English- man (so to speak) and his status in society, there is a very interesting story, which is, perhaps, not al- together credit- able to British generosity, and renders the Prince's present position more paradoxical than ever. Six years after the death of PRINCE VICTOR DRULEEP Ranjit Singh in SINGH. 1839, Lahore snr- WEIO IS /N THE BANKRUPTCY rendered to our COURT. troops, and we
appointed a Sikh,

protectorate, re- cognising Dhuleep Singh as Maharajah. However, four years later, owing to a rebellion, we annexed the Punjanb, forcing the Maharajah to resign for himself and his heirs his immensely wealthy inheritance, which has always been increasing in value and included the famous Koh-i-noor, in return for an annuity of £40,000. He lived for many years at Elvedon, and was very popular with all -from. Queen Victoria downwards, till his pecuniary resources failed and, the India office refusing to help him, te began to intrigue with Russia., Ultimately' he was Pardoned by the late Queen, but at his death in 1893 a financial re-adjustment was made, which only allowed his son, the prince at present in bankruptcy, £,8,000 a year. Large as this sum may seem to many, it does not go far with Oriental ideas of magnificence, and is but a poor scrap of such a great heritage; and, therefore, considerable sympathy is being expressed for popular Prince Victor Dhuleep Singh. There was no detailed disclosure of assets and liabilities, the creditor who asked for an order only proving a comparatively small claim: so poaoibly Ihe embankment way be only temporau.
