WE are glad to find The Downing-street that the conference • Conference.

_ between Mr. Casmana- LAIN and the Boer Generals in Downing-street reflects so much credit on all concerned. It would be important were it only for the emphatic repudia- tion by Mr. BOTHA of the irreconcilable ex-States Secretary Ram. But it has many other feattlre6 of interest. We learn, for example, froM Mr' BOTHA'S own lips that the:deed of surrender was not a matter of compromise, but was accepted by the Boers as the British irreducible minimum—to be taken or left. It is well that this should be clearly understood among the people of South Africa, because it demonstrates that the burgher leaders were fully convinced as to the futility o prolonging the campaign, and that for all practical purposes at the time of the signatures the Boers were a vanquished foe. It is desirable that Continental nations should understand the position of affairs, for their newspapers will then be less inclined to endeavour to work up a leaven of rebellion, or of its preliminary discontent. M 4 CHAMBERLAIN, too, was perfectly right in his resolve not to allow the discussion to revert to the terms of surrender, save only in so far as the Boers might hold there. was reason to complain of our interpretation of them. It will be noticed, how- ever, with satisfaction to all true friends of peace hat Mr. BOTHA and his friends avoided the cor.- troversial spirit. The tone was as modest and respectful as could be, consiE tent with their new dignity as British citizens; and it was as British citizens anxious to weld together the South African Empire that they made their propositions. How far that excellent aspiration is shared by the prisoners who are .now returning to South Africa' having many of them escaped most of the horrors and privations of war, must remain uncertain for some time to come. But the lives of the fighting Generals who met Mr. CHAWERLAIX last week have been fair and honourable, and we have not the slightest reason to doubt their sincerity. If they went back on their avowal they would be despised by their own people, and it May be taken for granted that before making the declarations they have in amplification of their oaths they have fully counted the cost. When one reads their plain, straightforward words, as expressed through the interpreter, one feels that these men are past the age of vanity or the cherishing of illusions. They have no wish to re-open old wounds; and although by their petitions they might have done so • unconsciously, if Mr. CHAMBERLAIN had not been cautious, it is evident their ambition is solely to make affairs run as smoothly as possible. They submitted rather than argued, and although undoubtedly they made some remarkable requests, the most important fact is that in no one case was it by way of dispute or with any suggestion of bitterness. The appeal on behalf of the Natal rebels was—to use Mr. -Boras's own word—one for" magnanimity " ; and the inquiry as to the security of tenure by the burghers was a perfectly fair and reasonable one. The fear that a system of expropriation is to be tried had a lot to do with the prolongation of the war, and that apprehension is dying hard. Mr CRANtsERLAIN'S conduct throughout this meeting was conciliatory. He promised to take steps for the recovery to the former holders of those farms in the Orange Free St ate sold under the proclama tion, and to inquire at once by telegraph as to some:alleged enlargement of rebel charges. It was,of course,impossible that the Government could saddle itself with pensions for the widows and children of Boers who perished in the war, but when the farming industry is restored we believe that the Boers will be both willing and able to aid their distressed compatriots. The loans which the Government intend will be a great assistance in re-stocking farms, and it must be remernbere.d that the wants of burghers are few, and the addi- tion of a few adult members to their families wil

not count for much. Perhaps the only unsatis- factory point in the Conference was Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN'S defence of the National Scouts. The Boers Who left the fighting ranks of the other side to join our soldiers in ending the war need no justi fication for what they did. But it is easy to understand that such people excite resentment among those who fought together to the end. General BOTHA complained as to these men being placed on the Compensation Inquiry Committees. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S answer was that they could not be treated worse that the burghers who sur- rendered later, and their number was not much above the proportion due to them. The Colonial Secretary should keep it down to the correct number. There should be no favouritism of these people for quasi-judicial work when so much depends on mutual confidence.
Mr. BALFOUR has appar
More Coercion.
ently quite abandoned

_ his idea of "killing Home Rule by kindness." He now seems bent on making it inevitable by coercion. The Crimes Act has been extended to six more Irish counties and also to the cities of Limerick and Dublin. That means the suppression of juries, the suspen- sion of the right of public meeting, and probably an end to the freedom of the Pdess. These are precisely the methods which the Cm.a has adopted to kill the liberties of Finland. They might be excusable if the publiC safety were endangered by the prevalence of out- rageous crimes. But there is not a county of Ireland where the amount of crime reaches the average that prevails in Gloat Britain. There is one town, indeed, where a good deal of rioting occurs occasionally; but that town is the Protestant and Unionist stronghold Belfast. As for Dublin, only a month ago Mr. JUSTICE MUG LIT at the Commission of the Peace, congratulated the city on its remarkable freedom from crime. The measure, then, is a political move, which aims at suppressing the land agitation led not so much by Mr. REDMOND as by the Liberal-Unionist Mr T. W. RUSSELL. It was taken at the instigation of the Landlords Convention, and is simply an incident in a -,lass war. It is more likely to pro- voke than to prevent crime. Ireland cannot be coerced into peace, prosperity, and loyalty.

ON grows almost weary Towards a of counting the signs of Compromise. the general disapproval of the Education Bill. After Bury, North Laeds, and Sevenoaks it seemed as though nothing remained to be said. But the Trade Union Congress has contrived to contribute a new factor. The Congress is, no doubt, a body which tends to be "advanced" in its opinion. But it has not the slightest desire to play into . .

the hands of the official Liberal Opposition —quite the contrary, in fact. Nor has it ever discovorod a Nonconformist bias. If the great controversy were simply a feud between one church and another, or merely an incident in the perennial rivalry of the " ins " and " outs " the Trade Congress would hold aloof. It only expresses the attitude of the men who are the parents of
the children round whose training the whole dis-
pute rages. It has not been content simply to re- gister its protest against ths Bill: it has actually

sanctioned the idea of refusing to pay rates should Mr BaLFona's proposals become law. After this one feels that turther agitation is almost super- luaus ; the country is against the Bill. Everything, in short, is ripe for a compromise—a settlement
_ which shall do violence to no religious convictions while achieving something for the neglected cause of Education itself, the last interest which men seem t 3 consider in the midst of all this

must have recognition by the state, equality before the law, liberty to protect, freedom to or- ganise, right to picket, and power to persuade." But how is this object to be attained? Undoubt- edly the best way would be to regain those rights through the same means as those by which they have been lost—viz, by legal decisions. Let judges undo the mischief that judges have done. But as judges are guided by precedents in the interpretation of laws,the tendency will be in the other direction. It will be neces- sary, therefore, for the old laws to be remodelled and for new laws to be passed,so that all doubtful points may be cleared up, and the status of Trade Unions put on a solid and unchallengeable basis. This can only be done by Parliament, and there- fore it is essential that Trade Unionists should devote their attention to the constitution of the next House of Commons. The first thing to be done, to quote Mr Burns again, is " the eviction, direct, merciless, and sure, of this Government of snobbery, jobbery, and robbery." This must be followed by the election of men who will act as honest " stewards for Labour . . . who regard Parliament as a sacred national trust, as a legisla- tive workshop, a legislative laboratory, in which discordant elements may be re:..onciled, class in- terests abolished, landlordism disciplined, pluto- cracy checked,and the social rights of the poor be harmonised and exalted above the privileges of money, caste, and property, that have too long usurped our Parliament and occupied the judg- ment seat of the British people." This is indeed "a consummation most devoutly to be wished."

sectarian strife. Tao Bill is undoubtedly Unity from beginning to end; but while opinions might have differed widely about the new machinery it sets up, there are not more than two vital points in it which need stir passions very strongly. The first of these is the proposed destruction of Board Schools, which have undoubtedly justified their existence, if not in tie more backward rural dis- tricts at least in the great towns. To retain the best of them would doubtless spoil the symmetry of the Bill, but that is a very minor considera- tion. In the second place Clause 7 must go, and the principle that representation and taxation go hand in hand must be respected. If the com- munity is to finance the clerical schools, paying for everything but the shell of the building, the community must have a majority on the Board of llanagers. Further, if some excellent suggestions could be accepted—made by thirty-eight Caurch- men, members of the Norfolk County Council—to throw open the teaching staff of these schools (excepting the headmastership) to Nonconform- ists, and to provide non-sectarian religious teach- ing for the children of Free Churchmen who attend them, peace might be attained.

But will Labour—organised Labour—achieve this ? It can, if it will. There are about two millions of Trade Unionists in this country. If they would all follow the example of the coal- miners, and subscribe a shilling each to a Parlia- mentary fund, they could easily meet the expenses necessary for sending to Parliament, and main- taining while there, a body of Labour representa- tives whose influence would be irresistible. But,as Mr. Keir Hardie bluntly told them last week, 1" before they had reform in the House of Commons they must have reform in the people's political thoughts." Working men must learn to think more seriously of politics than they now do. They most devote much time and energy to the study of their own affairs. They must learn what are the practical reforms which they need, and concentrate their energies upon them. When they cannot secure representation by men of their own class—direct representatives of Labour— they must not adopt the suicidal policy of refusing to support Liberals, who will help them, and of helping Tories, who will hinder them, under the foolish idea that there is little to choose between the two great political parties, and that it is " six of one and half-a-dozen of the other." However strong they may become in voting power and organisation, they cannot by themselves obtain an absolute majority in the House of Commons, and they can get no footing at all in the House of Lords. It is therefore obviously to their interest to secure, in addition to as large a direct Labour representation as possible, as many allies as they possibly can in the popular House; and these they can only find among Liberals. The hope of reform, for Labour as well as for Liberalism, depends on the honest and cordial co-operation of the repre- sentatives of both. They may not see eye-to-eye on all questions; but in opposition to class privi- lege and monopoly, and in support of justice, freedom, and equality, they are natural allies,and Toryism is their common fee. Toe constituencies which have returned John Burns, Thomas Burt, Henry Broadhurst, Charles Fenwick, Benjamin Pickard, John Wilson, Richard Bell, William Abraham, and Daniel Shackleton, set an example which Trade Unionists will be wise to follow else- where.

The decision, almost unanimously passed,of the I 'Trade Unions in favour of direct Labour represen- tation in Parliament will have momentous conse- quences. The lesson of Clitheroe has been well learnt by the organised working classes. It taught them that whenever they are resolved to have one of themselves as their Parliamentary representa- tives, and prove that they are in earnest, not by frothy declamation against capital and political oroganisations which have hitherto almost u opolised the field, but by the practical evidence of selecting their own man organising the work of the election ,and • all the escpenses which it '2lll paying their objet. From a entails they can secure purely partybploint of view this will tell most against theiet cause it will—at first, at all events—abe ptahr e y, ne- stituencies where Liberals are in a majority at y at- will be selected for Labour candidates, for in these the ground is already prepared for the experiment. But as nearly all the leading Labour men are Liberals, and will vote in Parliament on almost all questions in the same Lobby as Liberals, the loss to the Liberal party is more apparent than real. They cannot, and will not, dissociate them- selves from the many political and social questions, other than those which directly concern Labour, to which the attention of Parliament is so gener- ally directed. For them peace abroad, retrench- ment and reform at home, are matters of vital interest, and they will be found speaking and voting as Liberals, oven though they be not labelled with the party ticket. No Conservative Working-man has ever yet been returned to Par- liament. The Report presented to the Trades Union Congress last week, the resolutions passed by the Congress, and the speeches made by the delegates to the Congress, all give a guarantee that no Conservative working man ever will be returned to Parliament.

The proposed Higher Grade Elementary School in Warrington willprovide a muoh;neededlink between the Elementary day school and the Technical school A boy fresh from the Elementary school can hardly be said to be prepared to enter upon the study of technical subjects. The higher grade school will supply the deficiency and give the pupil a complete preparation for the life of a wage earner in industrial or commercial occupation, whilst avoiding purely technical instx notion. The cost of maintaining the school will be defrayed by means of the Customs and Excise grant, but the capital expenditure in providing a suitable building will fall upon the ratepayers. Until the plans are prepared and an estimate of the cost submitted, it is impos- sible to say what this additional wing of the Technical Institute will coqt the ratepayers. In neighbouring towns, technical institutes have been provided by local benefactors, but failing a Brunner, Gamble, or Powell, the whole of the burden in Warrington must fall upon the ratepayers.

The presentation of the annual report of Mr. W. S. Haddock on the working of the Warrington Corporation Gas Department, gave the Council an opportunity of ex- pressing their opinion on that troublesome and , not very profitable municipal undertaking. Alderman Roberts once again called attention to the heavy item of expenditure under the heading "repairs, iron, brickwork and mains," which totals' up to the nice little sum of £7,996 ss. 4d. Some years ago it was admitted that this item was merely a cloak for expenditure which should really be debited to the capital account. The explanation this year is that a good deal of the money attributed to " repairs ' has been spent on "renewals." This led Mr Alder- man Roberts to express the hops that the com- mittee had now got to the end of the ex- penditure on renewals. Those who have fol- lowed the history of the gas undertaking since the Corporation acquired it from 1 the gas company will be ready to confirm Alderman Roberts's assertion that it is one of the worst purchases the Corporation ever made. Not only was the purchase price too high but it was ultimately found that the site of the works in Mersey-street was al together unsuitable for successful gas making. The result has been that the Corporation has been called upon to build an entirely new gas works at Long- ford and considerably increase the capital account. This has hampered the committee in their endeavour to provide gas as cheaply as other Corporations. The price of gas in Warring- ton is s till higher than in neighbouring towns, and if gas is to maintain its position in competi- tion with other illuminants the price will have to be reduced to a much lower level.

The sad news reached Warrington on Friday that Mr. E. W. T. Richmond had succumbed to the injuries he received in Cornwall whilst cycling from Lands End to Newquay. By his death, the Richmond Gas Stove and Meter Company loses the controlling hand of its founder, and Warring- ton a respected and highly successful captain of industry. The deceased gentleman was a business man to the finger tips and In the present proud position of the company which bears s name is a striking testimony to his industry and perseverance. From very small beginnings he has built up a business of huge dimensions and his manufactured goods are to be found in every part of the country. By instituting a profit-sharing scheme he enabled his employes to share the prosperity of the business, and earned their respect and hearty co-operation. us career has been cut short before it rsached its climax and we can only lament the painful circumstances which have caused his death. Wide and varied is the circle from which will flow towards his widowi and relatives a stream of heart- felt sympathy n their most sorrowful bereave- ment.

The first and paramount subject for: the con- sideration of the Trades Union Congress this year was the state of the laws affecting Trade Unions. By recent legal decisions U ey have lost what they have long regarded as their legal rights, and their object must be to obtain the restoration of those rights—the restitution of the status quo ante the Taff Vale Railway decision. Till that end be 4iccom plished. the Trade Union, as Mr. Burns said in his Hyde Park speech, " rovst live, must grow,

div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

FIRE AT RUNCORN. About half-past nine on Saturday morning a fire broke out in an unoccupied house in Cansl-strees, Runcorn. The fire brigade were summoned and Superintendent Wright and his men :proceeded to the spot and quickly extinguished the fire. It seems that a beam had been set alight by the fire in an ad- joining house. The damage co the property was very slight. HARVEST FESTIVAL SERVICE AT RUNCORN.

Harvest thanksgiving services were held at the Primitive Methodist Evangelistic Hall, As bridge- street,on Sunday. The preacher,morning and even- ing, was Mr Morris Jones, of Liverpool.. In the afternoon a service of song, entitled : "An abund- ant harvest," was given by a special choir and orchestra. Mr 'AO A.ndets presided, and the reader was Mr W Handles. The hall was very beautifully decorated, the work having been carried out by Mr Hillidge, Miss Fox, Mrs S Woodier, Miss Bell, Mr McDonald and Mr H Wilkinson. IRE ACCIDENT TO A RUNCORN FOOTBALLER.

The accident which betel Tomlinson, the _Runcorn forward, in the match with Widnes on Saturday, turned out to be more serious than was at the time anticipated. it was stated on the stand that he had sprained his ribs,but subsNuent inquiries in official crarters elicited the information that one of his ribs had been broken by a kick and that he will be hors de combat for some time. CHOIR SERMONS AT ST. PAUL'S, RUNCORN.

The annual choir sermons were preached at St. Paul's Wesleyan Church on Sunday by the Rev W Terry Coppin, the nevvly-appointed minister. The , services were well attended. In the evening Mr Terry Coppin preached from the text" I will lay for a foundation in Zion a stone." Re pointed out that the superstructure of all buildings and of all work, whether mental or material, imperatively required e good foundation. It was impossible to accomplish any permanent work unless this was provided. Christ was the foundation st one of the ;vhole Chris- tian religion, and being imperishable the foundation would last when all other foundations had crumbled into dust. The choir rendered special anthems at both services. In the evening Mr John- son sang " Behold I stand at the door and knock," and Messrs Withington and Leathwood, Mrs Leath- wood and Miss Jones sang " Blessed is he that con- sidereth the poor." The singing was excellent. Collections were taken in aid of the choir funds.

div.p: RUNCORN NOTES
[BY A CORRESPONDENT].

Lovers of art will be pleased to learn that at the coming Aberdeen Exhibition Mr W H Leathwood intends to exhibit four pictures of Scottish scenery &c., and also one local view: Two of the oil paint- ings, " Kings college, Aberdeen," and " A view of old Macher," are taken from the artist's own sketches together with photographs taken by, perhaps, the beet amateur photographer in Europe, the photo- graphs in question having taken the first prize in the International Photographic exhibition held at Paris last year. The other pictures will be entitled " Scene from the Don "and " a view of Aberdeen." The local scene which at present only requires the finishing touches is a magnificent view of the picturesque portion of Frodsham taking in the out- lying hamlets. This, with the other pictures, is entered for the exhibition through Mr Leathwood'e agent Mr T W Hampton of Aberdeen. Mr Leath- wood is to be congratulated upon the success he has already attained se an artist, his ability as a man of parts being already well-known to the majority of Runcorui ans.

The Thelwall muddle still continues. In sheer desperation Mr Naylor has appealed to the County Council setting forth his grievances at length. This has had the effect of eliciting from the Runcorn authority's medical officer, another r-Tort. In this he states again that Messrs Long Ind Co. have nothing whatever to do with the outbreak of diphtheria or with the mysterious smell which comes and goes like some phantom of the night. The analyst employed by the medical officer certifies, according to the report presented, the water in the neighbourhood to be perfectly pure with the exception of Mr Naylor's whose water con- tains bacilli of the colon communis and stepti cocci groups which are quite sufficient to account for the diphtheria outbreak according to Dr Adams. The Council galvanised at last into action have decided to send a copy of each report to the Local Govern- merit board, the County Council and to Mr Naylor. ' Further developments are now certain, but what these will be, it is impossible to say. Meanwhile according to the report, Mr Naylor's water stands condemned. But in condemning the water it must not be forgottiln that the Council have not discovered the origin of the horrible, acrid smell which prostrates those who inhale it. The responsi- bility of "laying " this nuisance lies directly at the door of the Council, and why, in the name of suffering humanity are they not bold enough to make the attempt in a thoroughly business-like and practical manner ?

Of course if it can be conclusively shown, as the medical officer basing his judgment on the sanitary plumber's report, declares it can be shown that the drainage system of Cuerden Hall is defective there can be no doubt but Mr Naylor's estate is the main cause of the nuisance. The mysterious smell too, may arise from the entrapped sewers belonging to Mr Naylor. If this be really the ease,there can be no doubt but that Mr Naylor will be only too anxious to remedy any defects for which he is primarily responsible. Meanwhile it will be interesting to read the reply, of the Local Government Board, the County Council and Mr Naylor to Dr Adam's report The most adverse critic of the medical officer how- ever, will be ready in common justice to pay him a tribute of praise for the excellent report presented and the painstaking zeal hehas shown in endea- vouring to trace the seat of the evil.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

There was a considerable amount of interest centred in the match on Saturday when the two near neighbours, Runcorn anti Widnes engaged in a conflict. Still, though the game was exciting, it cannot by any means be termed interesting. The chemical representatives, notorious for their un- scientific piay and rough tactics, pursued their wonted style with the result that the game had ,to be stopped considerably oftener than once through someone being placed hors-de-combat. At the out- set the home team were unfortunate in losing the ' services of Tomlinson, who had to retire with one of his ribs broken. Naturally it was anticipated that Widnes would fairly romp round their oppon- ents and pile on a heavy score. But for once the unexpected happened. Time after time the heavy Widnes forwards rushed into the home quarters only to be sent back by huge kicks from Houghton or Jolley who never failed to find touch at the right moment. Indeed it cannot be gainsaid that had the visiting backs been better organized Runcorn would have been the vanquished and not the victors. The Chemicals over and over again gained possession out of the scrums and it speaks well for the defence of the Linnets that they successfully resisted the furious attacks made. The übiquitous Jolley was everywhere—kicking. collaring,fielding and scoring while Houghton baffled his opponents repeatedly in fine style. It would indeed be difficult to find a weak spot in the team Yet though the home team was a hard working one there were no fine finishes or touches save with the one solitary exception

div.head: WIDNES AND RUNCORN TRANS-
div.p: WIDNES AND RUNCORN TRANS-
PORTER BRIDGE.

Progress of the Work. • The construction and erection of this inaportsnt and interesting work has been well advanced during the last six months, and although considerable progress has been made on the site, still more has been made at the con- tractor' works. Oa the Runcorn side, a large amount of masonry and earthwork to form the new road approach has been completed, and most of the large cast iron cylinders which form the base of the towers have been sunk to the level of the rock, about 25 feet below the bed of the Manchester Ship Canal. As some of our readers may possibly not know the nature of the work which is being carried out, the fol- lowing brief description may be of interest :—The pre- sent accommodation for wheel traffic between Widnes and Rancern is either by Warrington Bridge or by the cumbersome ferry boats at Liverpool ; and foot passen- gers have to pay twopence, climb an incline at the I Widnes side, walk across the London and North-Western I Railway bridge and then descend by a long flight of I steep steps into Runcorn. TbP bridge under course of construction will do away with this uncomfortable unsatisfactory and expensive means of transit ; and passengers end all kinds of traffic will be conveyed across the river and Ship Canal under three minutee at the small charge of one penny for passengers and a varying charge for vehicles according to the nature of the goods and size of the vehicle. The bridge itself is really a suspension bridge without the usual approaches at each end ; which are costly in construction and in the purchase of the necessary lands and buildings. At each end of the bridge are two steel towers about 175 feet high ; these towers support the cables—which are about 12 inches diameter—from which are suspended two stiffening girders nearly 30 feet in depth. Upon the outer bottom flange of these girders are fixed ordinary rails upon which run a trolley 70 feet long, from which is suspended a car. This car will be about twelve Ifeet clear of high water spring tides, and will run from one side of the river to the other. It will be driven by electric niotors and will be capable of carry- ing at one time four two-home farmers' waggons (laden), and 300 passengers, and will make the passage from cue side of the river to the other in 21 minutes. The span between the towers is exactly 1,000 feet ; so the bridge will have the longest span of any bridge carrying wheel and passenger traffic in the United King- dom, and is only exceeded in span abroad, by the East River Bridge at New York. It will be nearly twice the span of :,he Menai Suspension Bridge. The t mars at each end rest on eight cast iron cylinders nine feet in diameter ; these are filled with cement and concrete and securely bolted to the rock. The approach to the towers on the Widnes side is by a short length of new road at the bottom of Mersey-road,and thence by a steel viaduct consisting of curved arched ribs of about 55 feet span ; I a similar construction is adopted on the Runcorn side, but the steel arched girders are sborter and the new road of masonry and earthwork much longer. The steel I cables carrying the stiffening girder are firmly anchored to lone cast iron plates and railway metals at a depth of I ovTertwi3oo rf iegeitaisnitoiatvhseastoslridorfoctkhisontevapcshosfidbe. ridge was Mr Charles Smith who designed one for Hartlepool about 25 years ago, but it was never erected. Bridges on this principle have been erected at Bilbao, Bizerte, and Rouen, and all work satisfactorily • the Widnes and Runcorn bridge, although constructed on the principle designed by Mr Smith. is of entirely different construc- tion from the above - named bridges and is more than twice the span of any of them. As there are no precedents for a bridge of this construction, the design and the necessary calculations have involved a large amount of anxious and serious consideration ; the calculations we understand, filling nearly 100 sheets of foolscap. The engineers for the work are Mr John J Webster. M.lnst. CE, of Westminster, and Mr John T Wood,of Liverpool, the resident engineer being Mr L H Chase, M.lnst, C.E. The contractors for the steel superstruction are Arrol'a Bridge and Roof Company, Glasgow, who had sublet a portion of the girder, tower and cast iron work to the Widnes Foundry Company, and the sinking of the tower cylinders to Messrs Holme and King. The contractors for the masonry and earth-work of the approaches and of anchorage are Messrs W Thornton and Son, of Liver- pool. In a few months when the towers are erected and the cables are being carried across, the work will be of an exceedingly interesting nature and will well re- pay a visit. If everything proceeds satisfactorily, as we hope it will. the bridge will be opened for traffic next Tear.

div.head: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON.

BARLESTOWN MAN'S " JI7BILEE " APPEARANCE Patrick Donoghue made his fiftieth appearance at the Newton Petty Sessions, on 'Thursday, when he was fined 103 and costs for disorderly conduct. The Chairman (Mr T J Gillespie) characterised his case as hopeless. GOOD TEMPLARY. The 1.0.G,T. hops of Eariestown Lodge, had their weekly meeting at the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, on Monday night. One new member was initiated. Arrangements for the3oth anniversary of the Lodge are getting well in hand. The pro- gramme for the evening was a fruit banquet with numorous readings. Bro J Clarke. T Dodd, J War- burton, J J Woods gave the readings. UNJUST WEIGHING MACHINE AT NEWTON. At Newton Hessians, on Thursday, before Messrs T J Gillespie, Dr Dowling, and J Unsworth, Wil- fred Bridge, farmer, of Newton, was charged with having unjust and unstamped weighing machines. Inspector Shepherd said that on the 22nd nit he visited defendant's farm,and there found a machine used for weighing potatoes. On testing it he found it 41b against the purchaser. A pair of smaller scales were unscamped.—He was fined 5s and costs in each case. DESERTER ARRESTED AT EARLESTOWN. At Warrington Occasional Court on Wednesday, before Mr Ziba Armitage,Elichard Baylor was charg- ed with having deaerted from HM S Pembroke, stationed at Chatnam, on the 13th August, he being a second class stoker. Prisoner, who was remanded to await escort, was arrested at Earlestown on Ties • day by P C, Irennie. AN OLD OFFENDER At the Awton police court on Saturday before Mr: Robert Stone, Margaret Huni,er, a notoriously bad character who has been in the hands of the police on several occasions was charged with being drunk and diaerderly in Earlestown late on Friday night. P.O Willis proved the charge and she was sent to gaol for 14 days. THE HARVEST. Harvesting operations in the Earlestown and Newton district are in a forward state, and a very large quantity of corn was garnered during the early part of the week. There is still a big lot out the work being hindered by the break in the weather. It is hoped there may again be au improvement, so that the harvest may be brought to a suceessful conclusion. ASSAULT ON AN EARLEsTOWN HOTEL MANAGERESS. James Lee, commonly known as " Tich " Lee,was fined 408 and costs at Newton Petty Sessions on Thursday, for assaulting Mrs Jane Kershaw, manageress of the Wellington Hotel, Earlestown. According to the statement of Mr H J Longton, who prctt.ecuted, and evidence of several witnesses, defendant was in the Wellington Hotel on the 29611 ult, when complainant asked for the evening paper that was for the general use of the hotel. It had been torn up, and when she remonstrated with him he %truck her several times on the back of the head and in the face, giving her a black eye. The beach said it was a most cowardly assault. BACK FROM THE WAR. THANKSGIVING SERVICE AT EARLEsTOWN. On Sunday afternoon toe members of St. John's servicelChurch Men's Bible Class held a thanksgiving in the Church for the safe return from Saab Africa of two of the c!ass mates, Messrs W Pilling and S Pickup. There wa, a very large number of people present,and the opening hymn which was sung with much pathos was" 'dome, Sweet Home." Another hymn most appropriate to the occasion Was " ittfe , home, safe home in port." An address of thankful- ness and of enconragement was given by the Rev. T R Matthews who selected for his text the word " rejoice " taken from the .sth's'iap of St. Matthew. Messrs Pining and Pickup were volunteers in the imperial Yeomanry, but they saw very little of any actual fighting. DEATH FROM OVERLAYING. On Tuesday morning an inquest was held at the Town Hall, Earlestown, by Mr Brighouse, coroner, on the body of a child named Thomas Jones, the five-weeks-old son of Peter Jones, collier, of 18, Athol-street, Newton Common,who was found dead in bed between 2 20 and 5 20 on the morning of the 6th inst.—Elizabeth Jones, the mother, stated in evidence that she put the child to the breast at 220 am,and when her husband came home from work at 5 20 a m he found the child dead.—ln giving effect to a verdict of "Death from overlying," the Coroner said it was no use talking to some mothers. At St Helens they were given printed instructions and provided with professional nurses. Notwithstand- ing this they gave infants liver and bacon. He was surprised some did not give them chops and steaks when they were born. NEGLECT OF CHILDREN AT EARLESTOWN. At Newton Petty Sessions on Tharsday before Messrs Gillespie (chairman), Stone, and Uneworth, John and Hannah Broster, of Lawrence-street, Earlestown, were charged with neglecting their children. Broster pleaded not guilty, and his wife guilty. MrJ W Knowles, who prosecuted for the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, withdrew the charge against the man,and stated that the woman had admitted neglecting the children, and the cause of the neglect was through her continual drinking. He suggested, with res- pect, to the bench that if they sent her to gaol for six monttis it would cure her, or else that they ought to commit her to the quarter sessions for trial with the object of her being sent to an inebriates home, so that she would be away from the accursed drink. She had been convicted in October, 1900,f0r a similar offence and sent to gaol for a month. After she came out she mended her ways for about nine months,but had since lapsed into her old ways and had pawned everything in the house for drink The bench sent her to geol for three months with out hard labour. PIPES IN A HAYDOCK COALMINE. At Newton Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Frank Reynolds, Robert Webster, and Joseph Smith (a Pole), were summoned for breach of colliery rules —Mr Arthur Ellis, who prosecuted for Messrs Richard Evans, said that a number of pipes had recently been found in the wood-pit in the work- ing places of the men, As a consequence, a most stringent examination had been carried out, with the result that pipes had been found on those men. No doubt there would be accidents, and if the men got their pipes into the mine the temptation to smoke would be very great.—The Chairman (Mr Gillespie) : Joseph Smith ! Is that a Polish name?—The Inter- preter: No sir, but that is the name he is known by.—Mr Ellis: The under-manager tells me he can speak English well down the pit.—The Chairman : Are the rules printed in Polish P—Mr Ellis • No sir. —The Chairman: I understand there are a great many Poles working in the colliery.—Hr Ellis: The officials take no one on who cannot understand Englisb.—The Bench fined each defendant 20s and costs. div.p: TES PROPOSED SR SWAMI WORKS AND DRSTROCTOR.

_ At the meeting of the Sr. Helena Health Committee, on Wednesday, Alderman .1 Massey presiding, the Town. clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board, iu reference to the application of the Corporation for per- mission to borrow £18,500 for the purposes of sewage disposal. The board sanctioned the loan, and made var- ious euggestions as to experiments which should be carried out ht order that adequate working rules might be formulated for the outfall works. Several minor alterations In detail were suggested and .the board stated that they considered it essential that some provision should be made by which the quantity of alkali waste-heap liquor being discharged into the sewer could be easily regulated and readily ascertained. It was suggested that something in the form of a special manhole or chamber should be provided and fitted with the necessary appliances for correctly regulating the quan- tity of the liquor to be added to the sewage in the settling tank. They also asked the Town Council to give an undertaking to erect the destructor within period of two years after the working of the tanks had commenced.—The Surveyor, Mr Bo m, commented on the effect of the letter,and said he thought it was simply impossible to regulate or ascertain the quantity of the alkali liquor which came from the waste heaps in differ- ' ents parts of the borough.—Dr Harris agreed with this. The surveyor was instructed to pr.pare estimates.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLES BY A CORRESPONDENT).
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLES BY A CORRESPONDENT).

The horse ambulance was used for the first time on Tuesday afteroon,and as showing how very use- ful it will be Ma case of the greatest urgency and requiring immediate transit to a hospital, I might point out that it took nearly an hour to get from the Town Hall to the Vulcan Foundry, the scene of the accident. Some people may think this is smart work, and pethape it is, when, before you can get the ambulance out at all, you have to hunt all over the place for a horse, even going to the extent of bringing the animal out of t'.e harvestfield Horse ambulances are for quick and rapid removal of cases of injury to some place where they can receive proper treatment, but I am sorry for any poor fellow creature, who happens to be so unfor- tunate as to need hospital treatment, if he has to suffer and wait for removal by the sarlestown horse ambulance. A man has time to die a dozen times over, whilst the ambultsce is hurrying (?) to his aid. How the delay is going to be avoided I cannot say,unless the Council keep a horse and man on the spot waiting for a job to turn up,but I think t he ratepayers will never agree to this. This brings to the front again the question, wad use is a horse ambulance to Earlestown?

The football season is now in full swing, but Earlestown's opening game with Stalybridge away, resulted in a loss of two points. Last year when they played the same club away they managed to secure a draw, but this year they had to suffer de- feat by four goals to one. This points to the fact that either Earlestown is weaker or Stalybridge is stronger than last season. Certainly Earlestown have lost the valuable assistance of Dawson, their capable and dangerous centre forward who has gone to Darwen. they have also lost Grime their goal keeper. In addition to this, on Saturday they had to do without Cottam who failed to turn up, and Pennington the clever half back, who was on the injured list. All things considered, however, the team played an excellent game and probably after a while, when each has become familiar with the other's play, they may give a good account of themselves. They have signed on a capable for- ward in Clare, a local lad, but he will only play as an amateur, On Saturday they play at home and have as visitors " White Star Wanderers " in the tie for the English Cup.

Newton opened splendidly. Their opponents were Tranmere Rovers, who are old rivals in the combination, and they succeeded in trouncing them to the extent of 10 goals to one, If this is the style in which Newton intend to go through the season they will be far away ahead of all opponents.

The Defence of the Mersey—Volunteer Sham Fights. On Saturday there was a mobilisation of the Liverpool Volunteer Brigade, which consists of the let, 2nd, 4th, and sth (Irish) Volunteer Battalions the King's (Liverpool Regiment). The orders for the movement emanated from Colonel E El Fitz- 1 herbert, the officer commanding the 8-40th Regi. mental Districts, whose headquarters are at War- rington, and who has full charge of all infantry troops in Liverpool, and his instructions were 1 swiftly carried out, the utmost secrecy being main- tained until the last moment in regard to them. 'I hose who were fortunate enough to spend Satur- day afternoon and evening on the Wallasey shore bad a splendid view of part of the movement. The sham fights on water and on land were watched with the greatest interest by many hundreds of spectators. True, it was difficult to decide who were the attacking force and who were the defenders ; but the public, putting aside such small details (to them)—and with the help of a few words from some straggling volun- teere—ilevoted their attention to the unusual sea- side spectacle. The first evidence of attack was fluted about half-past five o'clock, when from the Wallasey shore could be seen approaching the entrance of the Mersey a large gunboat. As soon as it was off Formby it opened fire, and continued storming the Lancashire side of the river during its quick progress towards Liverpool. Scarcely, how- ever, had it shown fight before it was fired upon from the Seaforth Battery, and so the sham fight continued until the gunboat had made its way opposite the north docks. The interest in this " battle' had hardly ceased before those on the Wallasey sandbills noticed some hundreds of volun- teers approaching along the shore from the Leasowe direction. They were the let Cheshire Volunteers, some mounted, others on foot, and many on their cycles. They had with them their Maxim gun. and had marched from Meols, and were in eearch of " the enemy." They had hardly reached the" Red Noses," New Brighton, before they fell in with the opposing force, and then ensued a sharp sham fight on the shore, which by this time was crowded with volunteers and spectators. The former were speedily joined by the Ist Liverpool (Cadets) and other Battalions. who had been scouring Cheshire waiting for a ight, in the thick of which they soon found themselves.

div.head: lEDUCLTION BILL.
div.p: THE lEDUCLTION BILL.

The following letter bad been received from the Brad- ford Trades and Labour Council :—The Bradford Trade Council is reluctantly compelled to again approach your delegates on the matter of the Government's Education Bill. Despite the fact that nearly every Trades Council In Great Britain has declared emphatically against the Government measure, Mr Balfour and his colleaguee have determined to force upon the country an education measure fit only for the middle agee. It is felt by the Trade Council that as we are being forced upon a last line of defence, vigorous as is this the last appeal we make to the workers, yet it is the only course which will meet the needs of the moment. We therefore urge the delegates to your Council to give sympathetic con- sideration to the enclosed resolution, which, if adopted, we ask you to send to each of the following:—Tbe Prime Minister, Mr A J Balfour, M.P ; Lord Londonderry Education Department • toe Government Whip ' - Lord Rosebery ; Sir Campbell Bannerman, M.P ; the Liberia Whip; Mr Herbert Gladstone, M.P. The resolution was as follow :—That this Trades Council is of opinion that all affiliated societies and Trade Unionists of Great Britain should show their dis- approval of the attitude of all those members of the present Pailiament who have voted for the destruction of popularly elec:ed School Boards. The Council strongly disapproves of the endorsem.nt of sectarian teaching at the expense of the nation and further ex- presses its condemnation of the means whereby these unjust and undemocratic measure were forceds through the H ouse of Commons. The Council yet urges upon. the Government the necessity of introducing a national system of secular education to be maintained out of the public funds and to be wholly controlled by the elected representatives of the people. It further declares its conviction that ateps should be taken at the next Parlia- mentary election to secure tht defeat of every member of the present House of Commons and all Parliamentary candidates who may not promise to vote for soon a so:ution of the Education problem' The SECRETARY said that those who had followed the Bill closely would be satisfied that the whole of the Trades Unionists bad condemned the Bill. It was not democratic enough, and Trade Unionists t cought that where public money was paid representa- tion should go with it. At the Trades Congress last week a resolution was adopted coodemning the Bill, arid stating on what lines the Trades Unionists would be prepared to accept one. The Council decided to adopt the resolution. " WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE," The Council decided to support the following petition to Parliament, organiz3,d by the Women's Trade Union League :—" That in the opinion of your petitioners the time has now arrived when the Parliamentary franchise should be extended to women on the same terms as it is or may be to men." This was all the business,

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
BAD CARE OF NEGLECT.

At the Warrineon Police Court. on Friday, Thomas Doherty and Mary Doherty. 16. Ship-yard. were summoned for neglecting their children in a manner likely to cause them unnecessary suffering and injury to health.—Hr Browne prosecuted On behalf of the NsPe CI —lnspector Hackett said he visited the house on April 25th and found the children in a Althy verminous condition and very poorly clad. The woman promised to make amends and when he paid another visit in May there was considerable improve- ment. In June he again found the children in a bad state bet the woman pleaded poverty as an excuse. stating that her husband had been nut of work for some time, but she also admitted that she had been drinking. On August 26th be again visited the house at 10.30 in the morning and the woman was almost drunk. Another man and woman were in the house and they were drunk. The house and children were in a filthy state—in fact they were just as bad as on the occasion of his first visit He believed the husband gave his wife his earnings—P ff Barnett said that shortly after mid- night on August 26th he visited the house. The I woman was sitting on the step drunk, with her 11 baby in her arms. The man Has also drunk. Two of the children were sleeping in an outbuilding, and two others were lying asleep on the cold tiles in the kitchen The children appeared to be famished for want of food.—The Chief Constable said the man had been before the court seven times and ths woman five times —The woman I pleaded bard for another chance, but the man had nothing to say —The Chairman said the Bench were agreed that the ease was a very bad one. If they sent defendants to orison, however, the home would probably be broken up, and they had decided to adjourn the case for a month to give defend I ants another chance of improving. If there was not a satisfachory Improvement at the end of that period, defendants would both have to go to orison. THg THVWT OP A HORSE AT WARRINGT.IN

At the •Marringten Police Court on Tuesday. William Mackie, last from Southport. was charged on remand with stealing a chestnnt mare. a horseoloth, and a bridle, of the total value of EV, the property of William Russell, cab pro- prietor, Bridge-street, on July 13th.—William Russell. cab proprietor, Higher Seven Stars yard. Bridge-street said that at 9 a.m. cn Sunday July 13th prisoner same to the yard and asked for a job. Witness told him that there was nothing doing, and prisoner then walked to a loose-box where he saw the mare in question. We asked witness if the mare went in harness and witness replied that she did. and he was going to drive her that afternoon. Prisoner asked if he could go with him, and witness said that he could,and told him to call at the yard at three o'clock In the afternoon. Owing to having , to leave town witness wai unable to take the horse out. On returning to the yard in the evening he found the mare was missing. Information was given to the 'police. He next saw the mare on tt e 16th July in a coal yard at Salford The horsecleth and bridle were missing.—Samuel Hall, yard- man in the employ of prosecutor, said that on Sunday July 13th, a man came to the yard and asked if Mr Russell was In. Witness said he was not. The man thereupon said he bad been there in the morning and Mr Russell had arranged to take the mare out with him. Witness told prisoner that be could not. take the mare, hut pris-ner said he would ride it over to Mr Russell. Prisoner Went to the stable, and putting a bridle and horsecioth on the mare, took it out of the yard, Witness unitd not identify the man, as he was very short-sightel.—Brnest Taylor, farmer. Stretton, said , he was at Hatton on the date in question when prisoner came to him with a mare on which was a horsecioth and bridle. He asked witness if he wanted to buy a horse, and witness replied "Yes if it is a cheap one." Prisoner said he wanted Els for the animal, and witness said it was rather dear, and he would net buy a horse on Sunday. He asked prisoner to whom the horse belonged, and he replied "IT° Mr Russell." He added that he and Mr Russell had bought a lot of horses at Wrexham and they could sell that one for nearly nothing. Witness mounted the horse and tried it, and told prisoner that it was not worth £l5. Prisoner then said h. mild have It for RIO. Ryentnally witness told prisoner he would have nothing to do with the hone. Prisoner went away. but returned in a few minutes, and ae.ain tried to sell the horse, but witness would not buy it. Prisoner offered to sell it for £9 les and on witness refusing to Mu it, be went away—Fred Taylor. brother of the last witness, corroberated.—Snmuel Hlgainbottom, coal dealer, Salford,said prisoner Came to him on July 14th with a chest-- sant mare. There was a bridle, on the animal but no horsecloth.He ask ul witness If he could leave the mare in the stable for about three-quarters of an hoar while he went for another Witness consented to this. Prisoner said he had ridden the mare from Knutsford. The horse was put in the: stable and prisoner left the premises, taking the bridle with him. Prisoner did not return for the houie.and on July 18th witness gave information to the Salford police.—Detective Meaeock, of the Warringt^n police, said prisoner was arrested at Southport and brought to Warrington Police Station. Witness read the warrant over to him and he replied "Yes, I took it away" He afterwards said " I lost the bridle and rug whilst asleep in a field at RuCklow Hill, Cheshire."— Prisoner. who had nothing to say, was committed for trial at the Liverpool Quarter Sessions.

He had to get a handcart to convey her to the Pollee Station.—The Chief Constable said he was positively ashamed of the shocking scene which the woman created in the centre of the town. Her language was " simply cruel." and a very large crowd was following her to the Pollee Conliffe said he took the woman to a cell at 8,45 and on vieiting her at 9.5 found three squares of glass In the cell door had been broken. The Woman said "I did it with my clog and I will do more damage if I am let loose in the morning. A REGGAE'S TEIREIT.-4aorge Davies WAS charged with begging in the Market-place at ten minutes to eleven on Saturday evening, and using threats to John Wood.—P.C. Clough said the prisoner was under the influence of drink. He had three halfpence In his hand and kept asking people to make it up to the amount f his lodging money' He asked Wood f tr money and when Weed refused to give him anything, he threatened to '. do" for him before he left Warrington. He WAS very violent all the Way to the Police Station, and tried to get away twice.—John Wood, 46 Golborne-street. corroborated.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for a month. SLEEP/WO It • RAILWAY CARRIAGE—A RaLwAY PEST.— Henry Livesey, was charged with being found sleeping in a railway carriage on the Arpiey Station siding, on Sunday morning. without having any visible means of subsistence. —Detective Howells stated that the prisoner was found sleep hag Inn third class carriage in the siding by a cleaner named Warburton. The matter Was reported to witness at a'-'it six o'clock, mad on proceeding to the carriage fotand prisoner was still asleep. On being wonted, he said he had no lodgings and tad corn. there to -deep. He at first Rave his name as William Jones. About a fortnight ago Warbarton turned him oat of a- second class carriage and he threatened to "do" for Wm. OR a previous occa.ion he was found on the sand hole at the siding. Re was a source of trouble and annoy- ance to the railway company —Prisoner denied that he had aver been in a carriage previously —John Warburton, a cleaner, said that when he turne i the prisoner out on a previous occasion he threatened to kill him. He said he did not case if there were twenty .• bobbies," they would not torn him out. He told witness he would wait for him to come on work again the same night and then throw a brink at his head.—Prisoner, who made his 10th appearance was sent to gaol for a month. _ _

He was playing the mouth organ and others were shooting and singing. Witness caught defendant and obtained his name and address. He gave addresses of his companions, which proved to be false. and summonses had net yet been served:—The Ohiet Con- stable said many complaints had been received about people going about dispelling the silence of the night by playing month organs and similar instruments. The month organ was particularly diabolical—Defendant was fined be. °Tagil Ormilsaits.-:-.4lary JaalBol2, 30 Lythgoes.lane and Marthailifewton, 24 Lythgoes-lane, were each bound over to keep the peace for six months and ordered to pay the 301t8 (12s each) for having committed a breach of the peace on August 9th. She went next door and receiving no answer to her shouts witness went upstairs and found the defendant on the bedroom floor She was black In tha taw, and foaming at the mouth. A FATHER AND DAUGHTER CONVICTED FOR ASSAULT.— John Earkell and Jessie Berkell, father and daughter were summoned by Bilbabeth Ann Nicholas for an assault com- mitted en the 29th August. Both parties reside in Gilbert- street an Aon the day in question the parties had a quarrel over the paying of dog licences. The male defendant struck the complainant in the o mrse of the argument and was assisted by his wife and daughter, the latter striking Mrs Nicholls with a stick.—The defendant denied the charge and issued a cross summons for assault. Evidence was called at length for both parties.—The defendants were bound over for six months and were ordered to pay the costs 13s In each case the charge against Mrs Nicholls being dis- missed.

div.head: DETERMINED SUICIDE.
div.p: DETERMINED SUICIDE.
A Big Dose of Carbolie Acid at Warrington.

The circumstances attending, the death of Patrick Kelly, forty years of age, a puddler, residing at 65, Foundry-street, formed the subject of an inquest con- ducted at tne Warrington Police Station on Thursday last week by Mr S Brighouse,County Coroner. Margaret Kelly, deceased's wife, said she last saw her husband alive on Monday, August 25th, when he turned her and the children out of the house. She next saw him when he was dead at eleven o'clock last Tuesday .aight. Deceased had for some time past been strange in his manner, but had never threatened to take his life. He had been drinking very heavily and " horse-betting." ' Witness beard that last Monday he broke all his furni- ture and threw it into the street. She thought he must have been completely out of his mind. I Ann Tooley, 63, Foundry-street, deceased's next door neighbour, said deceased came into her house at a quarter to one on fuesday afternoon and said "Go and see Maggie (his wife). I shall be dead in two minutes." She did not take any notice of his remarks, although the thought it was strange of him. kp the evening she went into the back yard,and on passinX the door of deceased's house, saw him lying on the kitchen floor. She sent for the police. James A Baine, chemist in the employ of Messrs Hill and Company,Buttermarket-street, said that at 11.30 on Tuesday morning deceased came into the shoo and asked for three pennyworth of carbolic acid. He produced a whisky bottle, bat witness told him they did not put carbolic acid into that kind of bottle, but they sold six- penny bottles of the acid. Deceased purchased a bottle, and when witeeis asked him what he wanted it for he said' To kill bugs in the house." . _ _

P.C. Hasp eared that at 10 15 on Tuesday night he went to deceased's house and found deceased lying dead on the floor of the back kitchen. Witness searched the house and found on the kitchen slopstone a bottle and a jug, both of which contained carbolic acid.

—Dat Smith, police surron, said he made a polt meet era examination of the body. Toe lips were slightly corroded and the mouth a little more so The gullet and stomach were very much cor- roded and the stomach was half-full of almost pure carbolic acid, which was so strong that it caused a sense of burning to the fingers on handling it. The cause of death was shock produced by the coProsive effect of carbolic acid of which a large quantity had been swallowed. In answer to the Coroner, witness said deceased must have swallowed about five ounces of the acid. As the jury were in some difficulty as to deceased's state of mind, Detective Barlow. coroner's officer, WBB called, and said he had known Kelly for the last ten years. He should aay that deceased was completel y mad when in drinking bouts. A verdict of " ouicide whilst of unsound mind " was returned.

WASSINGTON Y SWINTON.

The Werrin.e.,t-o-n-Fe7m—j-I.:;;;ve..d'vt;"S;Vii;t:on net Saturday to fulfil their first engagement of the season. The weether was delightful and a large number of Warrin4toulaws journeyed to Swinton to witness the match. Hallam was an e.heentee from the Werrington team, his piece et fall bank being taken by Knight. Wolff* being nnable to play owing to an injured knee There was also a &lenge in the hilt beak division, Onekworth taking the place of Allen. The teams blood eaeh other as follows :

Warrington I Knight, full back; Plah, Dickenson, Timken- hall, and Harris, tlaree-qusrters : Burgess and Daokworth, balf-bsoks ; Word:ion, Bosrdman, Swift, Edmondson, Fors- ter, Taylor, Roberts and Jolley, forwards Swinton : Traynor, fall back; Cooper, Valentine, Wall- work, and Barnett. three-quarters ; Samuel dad Slorgan,balf- backs ; liyans,ll Yates, Preston,Ponsfret,Jonas,Tickle, Barry, and Oheettrtm. forwards.

Mr J If Smith; of Widnes, was the referee. Fish won the toss and elected to play dawn the slope in the first half. Valentine kicked off and Ilockenhall returned From a scrimmage. the Warrington backs got possession and idockenhall was collared before be could part with the ball to Fish. Cooper next got away nicely and gained a lot of ground. Taylor headed a break away from the scrimm.ge and Dickenson gained further ground by a judicious klok. War- rington were now having the best of the play and Duckworth getting possession from the scrimmage threw across to Fish who had the misfortune to stfie into toech near the Swintur twenty-live flag. A passing movement between the Warrington backs gave Harris possession. but that player was unable to get away, he being too well watched by Barnett. Dicken- son was next prominent by accepting a miss-pass from Samuel, and it looked as though he would get through when he kicked to Traynor. Knight picked up the ball at mid- field, and made a good but unsucoessful drop at goal, add the brill rolled dead. The Swinton !forwards at length came away with great dash, and Preston had almost made his way through, when he was cleverly collared by Dickenson. Fish returned the ball and play settled for a time it, midfield. Burgess got his side peealised for picking the ball oat of the scrimmage. Both teams showed a disposition to find touch on every possible °wade' and sc,immagee were frequent. Samuel at length got away and after a passing movement right along the Swinton three-quarter line, Cooper got past Fish and looked a likely scorer when Knight tacked him finely about a dozen yards from the line. From a mark by Hookenhall 'play was taken to midfield where Morrison was injured daring a smart follow up. On resum- ing, the Swinton backs again got going, and Fish came to the rescue of hia side by making his mark in a diffieult position. A kick of Burgess's was charged down and play was taken to the Warrington 2-‘. Here Warrington were penalised loran infringement in the scrummage and Preston kicked a magnificent goal' This reverse spurred on the Warrington men and a passing movement was initiated by Borges., Hockenhall. however, held the ball too long before passing to Fish and the opening was lost. The Swinton beaks again, showed up Prominently, Valentin, and Cooper being very aggressive. Dickenson stopped a dangerous rush by the Swinton for- wards. Forster and Hdrnondson followed up smartly and Traynor was called upon to touch down Warrington now had another spell of attacking but could not score. Fish ma 'e a mark lathe Swinton 25 but did not attempt to place a goal. The Swinton men defended admirably. Fish put in a magnificent run right across the field, but was eventually tackled by Wallwerk. The venue was changed by Valentine forcing a spieneld opening for Cooper. who carried the ball right up to the goal line. Here a scrimmage took place, and Morgan taking the ball well kicked a fine goal. Immedi- ately after halt time was called with the score —Swinton, two goals (four polats) ; Warrington. nil. Taylor restarted and Valentine returned the ball to Fish who found touch, Swinton now gained possession from the scrimmages and the home hicks made good use of the open- ings which presented themselves. Knight defended vigor- ously and cleared his lines ins manner which called forth the plaudits of the spectators. Dribbling by Samuel and Tickle took the ball dangerously near the visitors' line, bat the drat was spoiled by a foal. Barnett, however, took the ball splendidly, and with a tricky run took the garne back to the old quarters. The left wing was immediately afterwards ' (conspicuous In keeping up the attack on behalf of Swinton. sad narrowly missed kicking a goal. Fish brought the ball out and before the home team was aware of it he was riming along the touch line in brilliant fashion. On reaching midfield he kicked into the open and collared rraynor before he conld return the ball. Cooper was next prominent with a dashing run and after evading several Warrington players he was at length collared by Hookenhall. Shortly afterwards the earns player received the ball from Valentine and scored the first try of the match. Preston kicked another goal. From now until call of time. Swinton maintained the upper hand, the forwards and backs showing superior combination and greater staying power. Valentine broke away in dashing style and scored a try. The goal kick failed and shortly afterwards the whistle sounded time, the score being Swinton three goals, two tries (twelve points) Warrington nil.

div.head: RUNCORN v WIDNRS.
div.p: RUNCORN v WIDNRS.

On Saturday at the Runesrn ground the above clubs met for their Initial enoounter. There would be at least 4,000 spectators when the gams cumin -need, tho weather being all that could be desired. Both elabs turned oat at their full strength, the game being keenly oontested from start to finish. Widnes won the tors, and after matters had been eontesterl at midfield Runcorn began to press. For some time Widnes were kept on the defence, and only the most stub- born resistance kept the line intact By degrees Runoora were forced back in turn, a splendid effort by Cullen jest missing a score. The visitors still continued to force ths play. getting the leather repeatedly at their toes. and making dangerous rushes for the line. Richardson brought relief, Inding touch near the corner, bat a free kick again brought the leather near the home 25. Jolley saved with a well-judged kick. A moment later the same player gathered from a scram, and after the ball had been handled by all the horn, backs Jolley scored between the posts Farmer converting. Widnes rushed away and for some time Runcorn bade lively timejolley relieving Butterworth next got the ball at his toes Kinsella saving in the nick of time Scrummaging still eiontinned to be the order of the dal, nelthev side making any head way. Cullen, for Widnes, was again conspicuous in baling his opponents, Houghton bringing off splendid saves twice in succession Owing to the absence of Tomlin, a home forward, who had to retire with the ligament of his ribs broken, Widnes pressed strongly keeping the home team penned up for a long time In their lines. A bit of exciting play between Jolley and the visiting backs ended in Aspey finding touch near the sortie, which nearly resulted in a seore Houghton marking at the right moment. The visitors had the best of matters to the interval but could find no opening, half time arriving with Runcorn leading by a goal and a try to nil. On the change of ends Cullen got away finely and passed to Bown who missed the pass with a clear line in front of him Serum after serum was formed. Douglas gaining po ion handed to Tilley who kicked across the field, Butterworth touching down In the nick of time. A passing movement initiated aby Richardson resulted in Jones get- ting away and knocking on when a score seemed imminent. Widnes was penalized for offside play, Farmer having a futile shot at goal. By easy stages the visitors worked the leather late the home 25, Jolley relieving. Widnes continued to get possession from the scrums but the defence was 1 more than equal to the attack. Flanigan got the ball smartly away, Kinsella saving and •ff ough.on replying which gave Beacom slightly the advantage. A forward rush placed the visitors line in jeopardy, Kinsella being tackled with the lbail in his possession by Lightfoot. After this Widnes had in lively time. Warder marking in front of the posts, Farmer kicked a goal. A minute afterwards Kinsella mulled the ball at midfield from a kick from Jolley. Flanigan gathered , the ball nicely at his toes and after dribbling half the length of the field touched down and scored a clever try, Farmer failing at goal. Rancorn continued to press in fine style , Houghton and Jolley ending touch over and over again grandly.—Final: Runcorn, two goals, two tries ; Widnes, nil.

div.head: ST.IMILTANS v, _BRADFORD.
div.p: ST.IMILTANS v, _BRADFORD.

This match took place at St Helens before 4,000 spectators Burtng the first half the visitors played against the wind and ground, but were prominent from the start, and in a couple of minutes Laidlaw scored a try aid Mosby kicked a seal After even play in the centre Liversage, passed to Barnes, who scored for St Helens. Lea failing to add a goal. Mosby

end Turner got along the touch-line, and the last-named got over near the corner, Mosby failieg at the place. The home forwards afterwards put la some good work.and took play to the Bradford line, where Ward missed the leather and Whiteley Immediately scored for St Helens, Lea again fail- ing. These were the only points scored in the first half ,ancl when ends were changed Bradford le6 by one goal and two tries (8 points) t• two tries (6 points)._ . . .

In the second half Bradford confined play to their oppo- nents' quarters, and gradually wore the St Helens men down• Ultimately some splendid passing between ffinton and H unbavin enabled the last named to floors near the poste, and Mosby kicked a goal. b. few minutes later Sinton and Dunbavin again ran down, and Dunbavin scored a try,Mesby adding a goal. The home forwards afterwards put in a good dribble, and taking the ball straight over the line Kennedy atmplated a try. and Lea, from a difficult position, kicked a goal. Jest on the call of time Pollard put on an additional try far Bradford. Mosby failing at goal. Remit :—Bralford 3 goals 5 tries (21 points), St Helens 1 goal 3 tries (11 points) Teams : Peadford—Ward, back; Pollard. Sir ton, Mosby and Danbavin, three-quarter backs; Marsden and lieseltine, half backs; Broadley, Laidlow Turner, B Smalls.. F Smailes, Sharratt. Dunn and Robertson, forwards. St Helens—Foulkes, back; Hunter, Lambert. Barnes and Ltversage. three-quarter bake; Done and Kennedy, half backs; Briers. Lea, Green Whiteley, Thompson, Maguire, Mercer and Presoot, forwards. /referee, Mr Y W Barker, Llversedge ; linesmen, Messrs W I. Britton. Leigh and El• Robinson, Runcorn.

div.head: SALranD V. ITUNSLET
div.p: SALranD V. ITUNSLET

Giving to the Hunslet team missing the connntion a late start was mole la this match, which was played on the Belford Ground, Weaste. Early in the game A Goldthorpe gave his side a lead by dropping a Sue goal, but this was only temporary, as T WlMama received a nice pass from Bell and scored e try. which Griffiths failed to improve. Before half-time, however. Brook scored a try for Hunslet, which A Gnldtbor ne nonverted, and Olt is were changed with the vislters leadine•b seyea points to three. linnslet had the misfortune to have one of their forwards hurt, and during the second half they played with fourteen men. For some time Hanslet. through the fine efforts of Mitchell. kept Salford out of their territory, and when throegnarter time arrived they ware still four points behind Bverything pointed to the visitors holding thrir lead to the fiaish, but in the last stages of the game Salford played up vigorously, and were at length rewarded by Shore scoring a try, but Griffiths failed to improve. Just before the call at time T Williams again scored and Davies kicked a goal. Salford this winning a sthbbornly fought game by one goal and three tries (11 points) to linnalet two goals and ens try (seven points.) WIGAN' • BATLEY.

This game was played at Central Park, Wigan,before 6,000 spectators. Wigan soon attacked, and Barr got over in good style, Bothwell gosling. On resaming,hostilities were more even, sad eventually a free kick resulted in Batley assum- ing the aggressive. Strong defensive tacitiee by Wigan,how- ever, kept their Iraes litaet, and Beesley at last changed the venue with a capital rush to the centre. Rouse next scored. and Batley tried hard to equalise matters. At last •akland get AL and enabled Davies to put on a smart try, the same player landing a goal. Brea play ensued, and then Davies broke away again, b 4. was quickly grassed. Barnwell next scored, and at half-tMe the some stood —Wigan, one goal and three tries: Hatley,one goal and one try. A resumption saw the home team going very strongly. but neat footwork did well for the visitors. Nelson gave Renee a chants*, which he failed to utilise, and hereabouts the visiting for- wards gained ground by several str nag rushes. For some minutes Batley confined operations to the Wigan half, and several times the Yorkshire men got in close prose mlty. but nothing tangible came. A free kick eased the pressure, and the home team at this stage had the upper hand, Halliwell sort ag and Nelson failing to convert. Later on Moisten- holme scored, and Really Wigan won by one goal and four tries to Batley's one goal and two tries. LEIGH • BROUGIITon ILNG gni . At Leigh, before 6,000 snechaters. The features of the game were the fine play of the L.igh forwards, who eons- pletaly overpowered the opposing front rank, and the admir- able use the Leigh backs made of touch. As Leigh controlled the ball In the sornmmages the Rangers' backs got few chances, and had to act chiefly on the defensive It is a remarkable feet that only once In eight years have the Rangers won at Leigh, and that was last Tannery. The run of the game was greatly in favour of Leigh, who fully deserved their victory, The alteration In the touch rule seems likely to prove very beneficial to Leigh. The Rangers started, and for a moment or two threatened the Leigh line. but the danger was removed by long kicks into touch, and I eventually, from a scrummage near the Rangers' line Moly- Ineux threw to Johnson, who passed back to Molyneux for the latter to score a try near the corner. Dunhavin failed to Wale a goal. The Rangers now rushed down into the Leigh half, and twiee from dim atilt positions did VV James try at goal, out avithout success. By long kicks Leigh gained ground. and Molyneux, Dunbavin. and Davies each tried to dreo a goal, but failed, and at the interval Leigh led by a try to nothing. On resuming Leigh had the slope in their favour, and they attacked persistently. Bennett. when at top speed, took a p ss from Dunbavin and looked certain to score, but Fielding checked him on the line. The Leigh half backs neglected their three-quarters, and instead of passing repeatedly tried to drop a goal, and Moiynenx at last acme- , pllebed the feat. The Rangers attacked, Itleyfes falling to gather the ball was rushed to the Leigh line where Ounbavin had a kick eharvci down, and W James soared a try, the same player failing at goal. Play was exciting during the last few minutes. each attacking in turn. Result —Leigh, one goal and one try (five points) ; Rangers, One try (three points).

div.head: HALIFAX V. HULL KINGIVINIX
div.p: HALIFAX V. HULL KINGIVINIX

Played at Halifax. In the first half Halite:lC had many hard lines before iforlent scored the first try of the season. which Little improved. Before the interval Hadwen added a grand try. Afterwards Rigg obtained a floe try, which was unconverted. galf-time ; —Halifax, eight points ; Hull, nothing. In the seomil half Lewis and West made a strong effort for the visitors, but failed to penetrate the Halifax defence Quick passing among the forwards ended in ttigg scoring, but Little failed at goal. More finished passing was exhilsited by Williams awl Had wen, but the latter collided with Guv. Result :--Halifax, one goal and three tries (11 points); Hull Kingston Rovers. nothing.
HULL V. OLDHAM.

Played before a large cr-aw.d. at Hull. Oldham did power- ful forward work. taxing Hull's defence. Jacques intercepted some paesing, and nearly scored for Hull. Oldham then scrummaged out of danger, and Pearce fought hie way over the line, a goal resulting. Jaeques smartly scored for Roll, the place kick failing. Half-Urns —Oldham. tiro polete ; Hull, three. The state of the game reet oven after Millar's resnmptinn, bat when Hall had a chance the bseks were again at fault. Pearce and Spottiswoode put in a rattling effort, and Hnll foil back. Later 9 Lees oilseed lowering the goal from an easy position. Oldham wsre having all the beet of it, their backs belng partienlarly quick and clean in all their movements. Williams scored after brilliant passing Ferguson adding a goal. Ferguson afterwards nude a splendid drop at goal from half-way, the ball hitting the posts. Result :—Oldbant two goals, and two tries (10 petals); Hull, one try (three points).

At Stalybridge on Saturday. The Revere had most of the play, and Wailea° had hard lines in not scoring. Taylor later missed an easy hence for the Rovers. THE COMBINATION. NEWTON-LE-WILLOW3 T TRLNMERE ROVERS.

The opening match of the Newton-le-Willows club was played on the new ground behind the Pled Bull Hotel on Saturday, the visiting team being Tranmere Rovers. There was a fair number of spectators present when the visitors kicked off. Soon after the start Birch scored for Tranntere, but the lead was only held for a few minutes Butler equaliz- ing with a fine shot. Returning to the attack, Houghton shot well, the ball travelling fast a few inches over the cross-bar. A penalty kick was awarded the home team a minute or two later but this was safely got away. Though the home team was now playing a strong game they had few opportunities and from a temporary break away the visitors got the lead again. A period of even play ensued, and then the home team began to assert their superiority again. After a capital run. Butler headed to Harsh, who cleverly equalized. Two goals each was the state of the game until the close of the first half. In the second half, Newton had nearly all the play and the result Was :—Newton, ten gulls; Tranmere, three. Butler scored five.goals, tfoughtor. two, Marsh, Harrison and Iter, one each.
