THE COUNTY SEASON CLOSED.
CHAMPIONSHIP AND OTHER PRIZE WINNERS.

The engagements of the fifteenth season, promoted by the Lancashire and Cheshire Association have just been brought to a termination. A very lengthy programme has been got through under quite exceptional circum- stances, which frequently have been anything rather tisan encouraging. The most coveted position of the year—the club chompionshqo of the two counties,carry- lag with it the Lancashire and Cheshire cup—has been wen by Didsbury. This team practically identical with that of Withington, inasmuch as their locale was shifted two years since, have secared the honour four times in the course of the fifteen yeari the County Association has been established—in 1888, 1893, and in 1893 res- pectively. Second prize, North VVarrineton, winners of the highest hononrs in the summer of 1897. Runners-up. Pend leton and Whitefleld.

div.head: Apollo Male Voice Choir's Success. . .
div.p: The Apollo Male Voice Choir's Success. . .

The Wirrington Apollo Male Voice Choir are to be congratulated upon the success which they ac- ehieved at the Prescot annual eisteddfod held on Saturday. Under the leadership of Mr Harry Berrey the choir gave such a creditable rendering of" The Spartan Heroes" (Dan Protheroe) that they ware awarded the first prize, value £lO. The adjudi- cator was Mr J H Roberts, A.R.A.M., of Liverpool, who said the competition had been a very 10,0,' one. is adjudication on the Warrington APS'"! Choir is as fellows :—" This choir is a er .1111' body of singers, with perfect control of the v01e39,' The opening nee vement was splendidly rendered. full tone, intonation perfect. The selo Wag very' well sung (soloist Mr H Berrey). The parting scene was most expressive with grand tone, as it should always be in movements ot this kind. The march movement was good, and from here to the finish was e grand performance." The judge remarked that it would have to be a very fine choir indeed to beat this one, and he had not the slightest hesita- tion in awarding No 2 (Warrington Apollo) the prize. The results were :-1, Warrington Apollo ; 2, Southport ; 3. Prescot. At the same eisteddfod Mrs E Wilkes of Warrington, obtained the first prize for the best drawn-thread tea cloth.

div.head: DEATH OF
div.p: DEATH OF
MR. E. W. T. RICHMOND.

It is with profound regret thatwe record the death of Mr. E. W. T. Richmond,chairman and managing director of the Richmcnd Gas Stove and Meter Co.. Ltd., who passed away at Porthcuroo,Cornwall,at midnight on Thursday week. The melancholy news was received at the firm's Warrington works at two o'clock on Friday afternoon and the flag was at once hoisted half-mast. The deceased gentleman was well known in Warrington, and had gained the esteem of all with whom he was associated. The employes, of the firm, edpecially held him in great respect and by no one outside his family circle will his loss be more keenly felt. The circumstances attending his death were singularly painful. Mr Richmond,accompanied by three other gentlemen bad been visiting Land's End, and on Sunday, gentlemen, 24Th, the party were returning en their bicycles to Newquay, to join their families. They took the road leading through Treryn and St Buryan, the route being very hilly at that spot. At the top of Treryn Hill, which is particularly dangerous,three of the party dismount- ed, but Mr Richmond continued to ride. He soon, however, lost control of his machine,the only brake he had on the hind wheel refused to act, and he went down at a fearful pace. About two-thirds of the way down the hill, Mr Richmond passed a waggonette, which was ascending the hill. The occupants, Mr and Mrs Fred Austen, of St James'- street, Penzance, their friend, Mr Broadhurst, a visitor' and his family, had just got out to walk, when Mr Richmond passed them, at lightning speed, just shaving by the vehicle, but not touching it. They watched his des- cent, and saw the machine strike a grass covered stone by the side of the hedge, the rider being thrown nearly five feet in the air, and turning a double somersault before he landed on his head. Messrs Austen and Broadhurst immediately ran to , his assistance, his companions being some distance off at the time, and found he was terribly injured. There was a hole in his straw hat where he bad struck the ground, and from his appearance they judged at the time that he was dead, his tongue protruding, and a lot of black blood issuing from his mouth. The front wheel of the machine was completely buckled up. Mr. Richmond was a heavily built man, which made the consequences of his impact with the ground all the more serious. He was immediately attended by Dr Atkins.who formed one of the party and was taken to an adjoining farm. Dr Jago, of St Just, was also summoned and every thing possible done to relieve Mr Richmond's sufferings. A telegram received at Warrington on Thursday stated that an operation had been deemed necessary and was successfully performed on Wednesday night, but that Mr Richmond's condition was still grave. Yesterday afternoon the news of , his death was received. It is stated that j before starting the ride to Newquay, the deceased gentleman promisel his friends not to ride down any bills, on account of the inefficient brakes on his machine.

_ By his death at the comparatively early age of thirty eight, 'ell. Richmond has been cut off in his prime. The deceased gentleman was an essentially self-made man, haring risen from the ranks to the position of Chairman of the Richmond Gas Stove and Meter Company. He was a native of Leicester and was born in 1864. He was apprenticed to the gas stove business ,and worked at the bench as a youth. Before he was " out of his time" he became a commercial traveller Meeting with considerable success, he at the age of 25 commenced a business of his own at Warring- ton. He did not start in a particularly ambitious way, and his first premises were over a blacksmith's shop off Scotland-road. Mere he carried on busi- ness under the name of "Unsworth and Richmond." His staff consisted of three or four men, and his capital was extremely limited. Under his capable management the business began to extend_ The little blacksmith's shop was soon too small for the business that came in. Larger premises were taken in Academy-street and branch works began to be established in other towns with the result that in the comparatively short time of twelve years the number of men employed by the firm bad risen from three or four to about 1,200. The firm at pre- sent employ 500 men at Warringtoraat Stratford 250. Chelsea 250, Oldham 50, and the branches at Plymouth, Bournemouth and Dublin another 150. This business has not been established without hard work and plenty of capable management. To thorenghly study business methods, Mr Richmond travelled through the States, throughout Europe Canada, and Egypt. He published a very interest- ing account of his tour through the United States, and apparently came back impressed with the importance of having up-to-date machinery if English manufacturers are to hold their own in the competition for the world's trade. He never had any trouble with his workers, and took a paternal interest in their welfare He worked on the principle that a successful business could only be built up if the employes felt that they had a per- sonal interest in the welfare of it. He was thor- oughly happy when devising something for the benefit of his people, and did his besc to make them feel that they were a part of the firm just as much as he himself was. After his return from America, he started a little journal called "The Richmond Record," for distribution among the servants of the company. In this little paper, items of interest concerning the company and its work, and news about the friends in the different brenchee appear, and altogether it is a smart little production. He was One of the pioneers of the profit sharing system in this country and every employee of the company is made prac- tically a shareholder The bonus was originally distributed in cash, but Mr Richmond found that this only temporarily benefited the men so it is now paid in ehares in the company. The principal is as follows ; After a dividend of PiX per cent. has been paid to the ordinary shareholders in the company, the men receive half the total per cent upon their wages: For example, if the company is paying a dividend of 12 per cent upon ordinary shares, a man receiving wages at the rate of £lOO per year would receive stock to the value ot £6,being 6 per cent of his wages. The next e ear he would receive 12 per cent or what ever was paid by the company on its ordinary stock. The following little incident is typical of the man. It was at the annual distribution meeting when he said" You know how difficult it is to save money." (Hear, hear). " Hands up those who, receiving eay, 30e a week, have saved 30s during the year Only two Ah I It is no laughing matter. When von are old and past work or when you are ill,it will make you cry rather than laugh !" The ern ployeea reciprocated his good feeling for them, with the result that the firm continually made headway. By his enterpriee and ability he has carried the name of Warrington manufactures into almost every corner of the land, and the firm has found employment for a large number of hands His visits to Warrington on the occasions of the annual profit-sharing distribution were always looked forward to with pleasure, and he invariably gave come sound advice to the employees. In June last, Mr. Richmond was selected as the Liberal Parliamentary candidate for Central Hack- ney. and these who knew him were convinced that he would have trade a good fight. He was a fluent, logical ond reasoning speaker, and had already addrersed several meetings in the constituency. He leaves a widow and four children, who, we a sympathy of War- I peoplerirnegTernP,w ilwill have in v etht heier heartfelt f elsadt bereavement.

lettero to the Ebitor. _— Important to Patentees. Sir,—Those of your readers who are patentees will be interested to know that in accordance with the Confer- ence held at Brussels about two years ago under the International Convention, some very important altera- tions in the International Patent Laws come into force on the 14th inst. The countries which have adopted these amended laws are Great Britain Belgium, Den- mark, France, Italy, Japan, Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Sweden, Switzerland, Tunis and the United States_ The three most important beneficial changes, and particularly to those taking out foreign patents, are the following, viz :- Ist. The term during which an applicant for a patent in his own country may file an application for patent in any of the other countries, and claim protection there from the date of the application in his own country, has been enlarged, and is now extended to 12 months, and no distinction is made in the case of countries beyond the seas. 2nd: The term of a patent obtained by any party en- titled to the benefit of the International Convention, will now not be limited to that of a corresponding prior foreign patent as has heretofore, in certain countries, been the case. Moreover, the lapsing of a patent through mon-payment of the renewal fees, or through any other cause, will not now nullify a subsequent cor- responding patent in anothrr country as has heretofore been the case in patents granted in France. It will, therefore, now be no longer necessary to file the appli- cations in any particular order in the above named countries. 3rd. The time during which patents must be worked will now be a uniform term of three years from the date of the application for patent, but even at the end of that term the patent will not be cancelled if the patentee gives satisfactory reasons for non-working. The following, countries which have joined the Inter- national Convention, but have not vet agreed to adopt the amended laws, are Brazil, the Dominican Republic, Spain and Servia. Austria-Hungary:and Germany have not yet joined the International Convention, but it is expected that they will shortly do so. There are also important amendments in respect of designs and trade marks which all persons interested should make them- selves acquainted with.—Yours faithtully, C. B. %UTLEY. Patent Office, 123, Colmore Rowe, Birmingham, Sep- mber 5, 1902.

div.head: ONS OF TEMPERANCE FRIENDLY
div.p: ONS OF TEMPERANCE FRIENDLY
s.poittirT
Visit of the Executive council to Runcorn.

Under the auspices of the Runcorn, Weston, and Halton branches of the Order of the Sons of Temperance Friendly Society a series of meetings have been held in connection with the visit to the district of the members of the National Division Executive Council. A demon- stration and public meeting took place on Saturday evening. The members of the branchee met at the Greenway-road schoolroom and headed by the Weston Wesleyan Brass Band walked in procession through the principal streets of the town. The handsome banner of the Order was carriel at the head of the procession by Bros. J T Fosekes and Joseph Walker, who were accom- panied by Bro. Heesom. The banner cords were carried by Eva Jones, A Shingler, S Hillidge, G Burrows, L Johnson, F Heesom and M Holt. The following officers of the Order followedr—Bros. W Gleadhill, 3Lw.P.. Hull; W J Wightman, M.W.S., Lon- don ; W Scott, M.W.A., Newcastle-on-Tyne; W Davies, M.W.C., Manchester; R Smith, M.W. Conductor, West Hartlepool; E Laugher, MW 5, Merthyr Tydvil ; W j Wightman, jun., M W P. Cadets, London ' • E Hallsworth, PM W P, Manchester; J Gib- son. P MW A M W, Newcast.e-on-Tyne •' J Sanderson, PMW P, Liverpool ; W Clarke, P 11,1 WS MW, Man- chester ; T Price, G W P, Crewe ; T J Holt, G 9, ante D Disbrow°, PW P. The procession marshals were Bros J Johnseu, F 9, Runcorn ;C P Bradbury, FS, Hilton; and John Brown, Weston; and the marshals for the cadets, Thom R Whyte and 'R Key. The number of adults in the procession was 256 and cadets 194. After making the round of the town the prosessionists pro- ceeded to Bethesda schoolroom, where a public meeting was held. Mr Harry Baker presided, and was accom- panied on the platform by the visiting brethren and the Rev J Osborne, and Bros Bisbrown and Cooke. The Chairman, who was cordially received, said he agreed most heartily with the objects of the Order. If by coupling a friendly society with a temperance society they could maintain temperance principles permanently the combination was a most excellent thing. (Hear, hear.) This was what the Sons of Temperaace had done. The Order was only some fifty or sixty years old btu it had a considerable hold upon the people of the country, and considerable funds at its back, and he hoped both membership and funds would continue to increase. He wished the Order and all its branches every prosperity. (Applause.) Br, William Gleadbill said though their first principle was total abstinence and they wished mostly for the removal of the great curse which was bringing such desolation to the homes of the people, they recognized as working men that a time would come when they would not be able to help them- selves arid that they must make provision for that time So they coupled thrift with total abstinence and week by week contributed to a common fund to prepare for a rainy day. It was because during recent years they had sent to the homes of their members at a time when they needed assistance half a million or money that people outside recognised that the Sons of Temperance had come to stay. (Hear, hear.) It was growing and increasing in its usefulness,and by the devotion of quiet workers in the towns and villages they were achieving a success year by year which exceeded the anticipations of their early workers. Twenty years ago they had 14,000 adult members. To-day they had 55,000. Twenty years ago they bad very little money mit by for a rainy day ; to-day they bad p 230,000. They had no poor and no rich branches. All were similar in position. The money all went into one bag and all the benefits were paid from it. Their object was to make the life of the people better and brighter, and he helped for an increase of work and enthusiasm in the Runcorn district. (Applause). Bro Hallsworth spoke of the work among the juveni'es. In their juvenile branches they trained the young to take an interest in teetotal work. It had been asked if they were making progress. They were. If they were not was it the publicans who created the public opinion .whichicaused the present Government to'prevent children under 14 years of age being supplied with drink? That was done on behalf of the child life they cared so much about. On January let drunken parents who endangered the lives of their children would be liable to prosecution by the police. The Government bad said that child life should be protected and if parents neglected their duties they would be brought before the magistrates. All clubs would shortly have to be regis- tered. Were these things because the brewers and publicans were agitating for them? No; these reforms were due to the pertinacious work of the temperance party. (Hear, hear.) They were never defeated. They had been repulsed many times, but they were soon back again pegging sway at the same old thing, that where there was drink there was danger. The Church was practically with them to-day and they were delighted. Once the deers of the Church were closed to them but it as not so now. They were on the winning side, and the Church recognized with them that the only safety for the people lay in total abstinence. (Applause). Bro W J Wightrnan, jun., chief of the Cadet officers, said the membership of this branch of the organization was 30,000. The enterprising business man looked care- fully after the juniors in his employ, for he knew that they were to follow in the plazes which in time became vacant at the older bands passed away. So they in the temperance movement looked well after the young. The chief dividend they as Sons of Temperance received for their work was the enrolment of boys and girls at the earliest possible age and their careful training. Applause.) Addresses were also delivered by Bros W Scott, E Laugher, and W 3 Wightman. Bro Cooke proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman, and announced that it was his intention to become an honorary member of the Order. (Applause). Mr Bishrown seconded, and the vote was heartily carried. ei The meeting cicseid with the singing of the Doxology. On Sunday sermons were preached in the Greenway- rnad Primitive Methodist Chapel, Weston Point. and Weston WeslPcso Chenele, Halton-road weslevan Chapel, and 13nthentia Congregational Chapel by Bros Wighttnan, Smith. Davies. and Losieber, and addresses were given at Weeon Wesleyan fiuneay Scheel, Run- corn Pariah Chureh Sisnday School, Weston P-int Sunday School, ard Brunswick Sunday School. by Brns Smith. Davies, Wightmen, and Hallswerth. The Brunswick V.S.A. Society meeting Vivaq aiSn visited, and addresses were given by members of the Council.

div.head: IThe Borough Surveyor's Duties.
div.p: IThe Borough Surveyor's Duties.

The report of the special committee appointed to con- sider and report upon the re-organization et the Borough ' Surveyor's Department, as approved by the various committees, has just been issued. The committee con- sisted of Aldermen Heaton, Sutton, Monks, Csuncillors Tinnion and Greening. They recommend that the duties of the Borough Surveyor be defined as far as practicable, and without removing the supervision and responsibility of the Surveyor they are of opinion that in addition to the general duties appertaining to the office of Assistant Surveyor certain specific duties should be assigned to that office, and that certain other duties of a clerical or routine character might with advantage and safety be given to other members of the Surveyor's staff. By the terms of his appointment the Borough Surveyor was not required to carry out any architec- tural work. Without precluding any committee from requiring the Surveyor to perform any duty or to carry out any work, it has been found convenient to defuse the duties of the Surveyor with regard to the duties of a continuing character under the control of several committees._

-GENERAL DUTIES OF THE BOROUGH SURVEYOR. After defining the duties with reference to matters under the control of the Paving and Sewerage Commit- the, the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee, the Health Committee, the Finance and Estate Commit- tee, the Town Hall, Park and Baths Committee, the Markets Committee, and the Rivers Committee the com- mittee define the general duties of the Borough Surveyor to be as follows : To report upon all matters specially referred by the Council or by any Committee to him. To attend the meetings of the Council and of the Street Improvement and Lighting, Paving and Sewer- age, Town Hall, Park and Baths, Rivers, and General Purposes Committees and to attend meetings of ether Committees when required. :43; To devote the whole of his time to the duties cf his office, and not to be engaged directly or indirectly in any profession or employment. To be solely responsible for the proper and efficient conduct of the business of bie department. Not to take or accept for his own use or benefit either ' directly or indirectly any fee,emolument, giit,perquisite 'or any charges or remuneration (save his salary) or any discount or commiesion of any account whatsoever. Not to become suret7 for any person or persons in respect of or for the payment :of any sum or sums of money. To reside within three miles of the Town Hall.

I To obtain tenders for all work to be performed and all goods to be supplied under the direction of the several committees requiring the same and to be respon- sible for the carrying out and due execution of all con- trastel.

To have charge of and be responsible for all buildings and property not specially referred to any other officer of the Corporation. To keep proper books and accounts and to prepare plans, estimates and specifications of all work of the Corporation within the province of the Borough Sur- veyor • . _

measure up all work done for the Corporation and to prepare the necessary certificates fo: the payment of moneys on account of contracte.3 To examine and certify all accounts for payment, and transmit the same to the Borough Treasurer. To furnish to the Borough Treasurer such iafortnation as will enable him to prepare his monthly and other statements on the estimates of each Committee. To prepare and certify all apportionments for Private Street Works and other Private Improvement expenses. To keep accurate records and 'plans for permanent reference of all buildings and other properties of the Corporation, and to be responsible for the safe custody thereof.

To watch all notices of Parliamentary Bills and Orders and to report upon all matters affecting the interests of the Borough. To carry out all bye-laws and the provisions of all local and general acts so far as the same are within the province of the surveyor. To be in attendance at his office daily between the hours 10 and 11 a.m. DUTIES OF THE ASSISTANT' SURVEYOR. 1 To act under the direction and control of the Ii surveyor.
, 2 To be responsible for the conduct of the drawing office and for the accuracy of all plans prepared therein. 3 To prepare the necessary plans of all private street works.
4. To obtain accurate lists of all owners and to see:to le proper apportionment of expenses.

. . 5 To measure up private street works and works executed under contract, and to prepare all final appor- tionments of expenses and certificates for work done. 6 Tp be responsible for levels of all sewers and th preparation of plans therefor. _ _ _ _

7 To see tha't the Bye-laws and Acts of Parßarnet' , relating to the Surveyor's Department are complied with, and to report to the Borough Surveyor upon any infringement thereof. '294g 4an 8 To attend committee meetings when required, and in the absence of the Borough Surveyor to take charge of the staff and workmen and to be responsible for the efficient discharge of the duties of the department. 9 To devote the whole of his time to the duties of his office, and not to be engaged directly or indirectly in any other profession or employment. 10 Not to take or accept for his own use or benefit either directly or indirectly any fee, emolument, gift, perquisite or any charges or remuneration (save his salary) or any discount or commission of any account whatsoever.

11 Not to become surety for any person or persons ,in respect of or for the nayment of any sum or sums of money. 12 To reside within three miles of the Town Hall. 13 To be entitled to two weeks' vacation.
14 To attend at the office from 9 a.m. to 5.30 p.m. DUTIES OF BUILDING INSPECTOR.
I To examine and report on all building plans sub- mitted for the approval of the Street Improvement Committee.
2 To report to tbe Borough Surveyor on all danger- ous or dilapidated buildings, Ize., and to serve notice of same on owners.

3 To inspect all new badings, drains, damp-proof courses. foundations, &c., and report on same to the Borough Surveyor. 4 To prepare plans for the Medical Officer of Health of all insanitary dwellings, Acc., and report on same. 5 To prepare certificates of approval of plans and for habitation of houses.
Duties Noe 9to 12 of Assistant Butveyor to apply to the Building Inspector. DUTIES OF RIVER INSPECTOR.

To survey, plan, and carry out all work in -connection with the river especially in seeing that the provisions of the Manchester Ship Canal Act and of the agreement are carried out and to keep daily records of the sat e of the river and to report monthly to the Rivers C)mmittee. DRAUGHTSMAN. To carry out general work of office in preparation of street and drainage plans, and generally act under Chief Assistant.

div.head: CLERK.
div.p: CLERK.

To be responsible for all letters and correspondence. Shorthand Clerk and Typist. To be responsible for all material books and accounts, examining same before passing on to the Borough Sur- veyor /or cerrifying for payment. General Clerk's work. JUNIOR CLERK.
To asiist Clnk in his work. Shorthand Clerk and typist. GENERAL.

The Committee are of opinion that the borough sur- veyor requires further assistance in his drpartment, and that the Paving and Sewerage Committee should be requested to take into consideration the question of the outside staff of the surveyor's department. The report was approved at the meeting of the Town Council on last week.

div.head: Lymm Horticultural Society.
div.p: Lymm Horticultural Society.

The old Lymm Horticultural Society was lately revived and the first annual show was held in the Drill Hall, on Saturday. Every effort to secure a good exhibition bad been made by a representative committee, consisting of Messrs J Brazendale, L Bradburn, J Driver, W Driver, S Davies, 3 Hatton, G Kennerley, J Oxton, F 0 Smith. H Wingrove, and T Winstanley. The number of entries were some- what disappointing, though the quality of the ex- hibits left little to be desired. The judges were Messrs W Coulson (lhelwall) and Poulton (Grappen- hall), whose decisions gave general satisfaction. In the evening Mrs Palmer graciously presented the prizes to the successful exhibitors, and Major W P Mac Kendrick, the president, congratulated the pociety on their excellent show, which he hoped another year would be more liberally supported both financially and by a more extended entry. Mr J Palmer complimented the committee on the diffi- culties they had surmounted, and wished them further successanother year. Sergeant H 44 ingrove proved a very capable and efficient secretary. A Runaway Horse. Shortly after noon on Tuesday, a horse attached to a small gig, belonging to George Hatton, farmer, Lyulni, took fright in front of the King's Arms, Buttermarket-street, Warrington, while a 'bus was being turned round. It bolted along the street. but Police-constable Whitley caught hold of the bridle, and, after running along the street about twenty yards, be brought the horse to a etandstill. No damage was done.
LADIES' MARKET BASEETS—Wusum BEavrtax, 21.Batterroarket-etreet, Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: Borouczl
div.p: Borouczl
THE EXAMIN ER FRIDAY SEPTEMBER 12, 1902
RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the above authority was held at Dutton on Tuesday. Mr A R Norman (vice- chairman) occupied the chair, and there were also pre- sent :—Dr Gastaldi, Messrs T Wood, J Lea, J Douglas, the members of the Rural District Council with Messrs G F Ashton (clerk), W E Hough (assistant clerk, J Cunnah (master), T Cooke, J Deprez and J Riley (relieving officers).

div.head: COUNTY ASYLVII.
div.p: THE COUNTY ASYLVII.

The Clerk reported that the Rev Dr. Gastaldi, Mr Roylance and himself had visited the Chester County Council and seen the inmates sent from their union en the Bth of September. The Committee were pleased with the manner in which the institution was conducted and the way in which the inmates were treated. At present there were 38 females and 29 males chargeable to the union, there being one attendant to every ten patients. The expenses of the committee amounted to £2 101. Dr. Gastald, in moving the adoption of the report,said the ;people were extremely well looked after and every- thing was satisfactory. They ascertained that it would net have been possible to have aeon the inmates if thee had not sent them an intimation. This was due to the fact that the patients were situated in different quarters of the building and they had to get them together before- hand to be seen by the Committee. Mr Roylance seconded and the report was confirmed.

div.head: ESTIMATES'
div.p: THE ESTIMATES'

The Clerk submitted an estimate of the contributions, required from the various parishes in the Union towards the rate for the het year ending Lady Day, 1903. The total capital for the current half-year was £8,927, and the Probable expenditure £7,454 leaving a balance of £1,473. The probable expenditure during half-year ending Lady Day 1903 was as follows :—Common charges, £2,630 ; county rate, £3,099 ; balance and con- tingency, £2,361, total £8,090. After deducting th. probable, balance there remained a sum of £6,617 required from the overseers. A rate of 70 in the £on the assessable value £211,399 would produce £6,606, and it wag recommended that a call for £6,617 (being equal to the call for the corr2sponding period of last year) be made upon the overseers. The amount of con- tribution required from the various parishes was as follows :—Acton Grange. £114; Alvan- ley, £5l •, Antrobus, £79 ; Appleton. £167; Aston, I£l4o ; Aston Grange, £l6 Bartington, £2O ; Budworth, £B4 ; Clifton, £ll4 ; Crowley, £4l ; DaresburY, £34 ; Dutton, £244 ; Frodsharn, £360 ; Frodsham Lordship, £220 ; Granpenhall, £224 ; Halton, £154 ; Hatton, £49 ; Helsby, £275 ; Keckwick. £97 ; Kingsley, £164 ; Kingswood, £45 : Latchford (Without), £77 •, Manley, £5O ; Moore, £137 ; Newton- by-Daresbury, £3B ; Newton-by-Frodsham, £27; Nor- ley, £lO6 ; Norton, £175 ; Preston-o'-th'-Hitl, £llO ; Runcorn, £1,734 ; Sevenoaks, £2B ; Stockharn, £24 ; Stockton Heath, £295 ; Stretton. £6O; Sutton, £199 ; Thelwall, £l4B ; Walton Inferior, £l4B ; Walton Superior, £65 ; Weston, £416 ; Whitley Inferior, £52 ; Whitley Superior, £56. Mr Woodward, in moving the confirmation of the estimates, said that the rate was the same as last half year. .
Mr Wright seconded, and the recommendation was approved.
FINANCE.

Mr Woodward repotted that the ou'l Payments were as follows : Runcorn, £9O ; Frodsham,£23 ; Budworth, £lO. The balanco from last meeting was £35 3s 10d ; receipts, £BB7 3s 2d ; cheques drawn that day, £155 ; balance, £787 74. The report was adopted. A ROYAL COMMUNICATION.

At the time of the King's illness the Board forwarded a message of sympathy to his Majesty, and the follow- ing reply was received from Mr A Akers Douglas, of the some Office :—1 have had the honour to lay before the King the loyal and sympathetic resolution adopted at the meeting of the Guardians of the Runcorn Union, on the occasion of his Majesty's severe illness. His Majesty was pleased to receive the same very graciously.
AN APPLICATION.

Messrs C J Bushell (chairman), James H Ismay (hon treasurer) and T Hoyden (bon secretary) wrote anneal- ing for donations towards the £4,000 required by the 'committee for the building and equipment of a training Briaantine for the Indefatigable. Nothing was done in the matter. QTJESTICN OF VACCINATION.

The Local Government Board forwarded a copy of the decision a the High Court of Justice in the case of Moore v Keyte in relation to a conviction by the magis- trates of Leicester for baying neglected to cause a child to be vaccinated six months after its birth. This stated that the statute imposed upon the public vaccinator the duty of going to the home of the child, and imposed on the psrmt the duty of causing his child to be vac- cinated.

THE CLERK'S REMUNERATION. The Clerk said that 3i years ago when he Was ap- pointed clerk they were pleased to appoint a joint com- mittee between the District Courierl and the Guardians as to the salary that should be offered. The committee very properly reported that his salary should not be as great as that paid to his late father. Since he had re- ceived th•t apnoin,ment the work of the Council and the Guardians had materially increased and naturally the expenses of his office had increased in proportion. Therefore his actual remuneration was not nearly so much as when he received his appoint- ment. He wished therefore to ask that the Board would kindly consent to appoint a committee to meet u ith a committee of the Rural District Council to inquire into the question of hi a remuneration and report whether it was a fair time that some alteration should be made.
The Chairman said it was a reasonable request for the Clerk only asked that a committee should be appointed to go into the matter.
Mr Linker moved that Meqrs Taylor, Linakor, Baxter, Knowles, Pining, Chadwick, Wright and Wood- ward form the committee.
Mr. Woodward seconded and the proposition was passed,
Accident at the Vulcan.

On Tuesday afternoon William Burgess, residing in Mercer-street, Newton, and employed as a fitter at the Vulcan Foundry, met with an accident by which the heel of one of his feet was torn away. He was engaged at a travelling crane,and in pulling over a lever his foot slipped and the heel got fast in the cogs 'of a wheel. He was re- moved in the horse ambulance to the Warrington Infirmary after his injuries were dressed by Dr Mounsey,

ASK for CUNNINGHAMS HIGH-CLASS MINHHAL WATEFS,—Advt Ship Canal Development. The negotiations for the development of the direct American trade with Manchester have made steady progress, and signs are not wanting that the Ship Canal will soon be utilized to a far greater extent than at present in connection with the in- terchange of the products of the two countries. The development of the city end of the Canal by the erection on its banks of warehouses and works of different kinds proceeds satisfactorily. The latest announcement of this sort has reference to the establishment of a patent fuel manufactory at Cadishead. The fuel is stated to be much cheaper than coal, and a large shipping company has inter- ested itself in the scheme. An attempt to still further increase the carrying trade between the Canal and North America is to be made by Mr R Bram Stoker, the managing director of the Man- chester Lieers, Limited. Mr Stoker will proceed to Canada, and from there he will visit New Orleans, Chicago, and Pensacola. FOOT COMFORT is a bargain at any price, wear ALF TA.YLOW3 wonderful boots.—Advt.

BLUR BELL POLISH and Symuz for Glossing— Wm BEtWICX, 21, Enttermarket-at, Warrington I Advt.. Horse Sold to be Destroyed, but Landed at Antwerp. Charles Kelly, of Patricroft, was charged at Newton Petty Sessions on Thursday with cruelty to a horse. Constable Sefton said that on the after- noon of Tuesday, August 12th, he saw defendant walking an aged grey mart along High-street, Newton, at the Newton fair, offering it for sale. It was lame in the off hind leg. Inspector Print,of the Royal Society, said defendant told him later he had sold the horse for 36i to be destroyed. The society had since learned that the horse had landed at Antwerp, and had not been destroyed. The Chair- man said it was a very bad case. Defendant bad promised to destroy the horse, but had sold it to make a profit. He would be fined 20s and costs. At the same court, William Forster and William Swift were charged with a similar offence on the 29th ult. Constable Benson said that on Priday,the 20th ult, he met the defendant Swift in charge of a horse attached to a cart in High-street, Newton. It was , completely done up. There was a raw wound,about I the size of a five-shilling piece, under the collar,and another raw wound, about the size of the palm of a man's hand, under the saddle, which was covered with blood and matter. Inspector Print gave evi- dence. The bench fined Forster 20s and costs and Swift 5s and costs. FOR GOOD TWlRRS—Wittiaat BEsalca, 21, Buttermarket-etreet, Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: 1 HE THELWALL NUISANCE.
div.p: 1 HE THELWALL NUISANCE.
The County Council Intervenes.
Another Report from Dr. Adams.

The subject of the alleged nuisance at Thelwall was again discussed at the meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council, held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Mr Potts, clerk to the County Council wrote enclosing ' a copy of letter fromPlr R AlNaylor which would receive the consideration of the Public Health Committee on the 24th October and asking for the observations of the Rural District Council upon the stataments contained in the letter.—Mr Naylor's letter dated August 28th, London, was to the effect that through the dreadful scourge to the locality he had been compelled to close his residence Cuerder Hall. He bad almost lost his life on two Occasions through inhaling the poisonous stench while he, his sister, and his visitors had been made seriously ill in consequence of the stench. Recently be bad received three letters from Mrs. Grimshaw, Thorn Lee, Ashton- on-Mersey, Dr Robert Marshall, a medical officer of health and Miss Stumm, Harrogate. The letters all agreed that a poisonous efluvia was in the neighbourhood of Thelwall. Mr Naylor, continuing, traced the efforts of the Rural District Council in grappling with the nuis- ance, quoting the reports of Dr Penny. A letter was also quoted from Mr Naylor' coachman in which he alleged that the smell came from the tannery and that he bad buried three little children in consequence of the vile smells. Mr Naylor concluded with the hope that the serious matter would occupy the attention of the County Council and alleging the Cause of the nuisance to be th‘ Tannery. On the ssme subject Messrs Long and Sons. Grappen- hall,wrote pointing out that according to the press re- ports they were accused of being accountable for the delay with the completion of the work at the brook. They had al ways been opposed to the closing in of the original channel down which the tanyard efluent flowed. On condition that they were guaranteed from any annoyance they had withdrawn their opposition. The workmen there employed were now complaining of the bad smell emanating from the Thelwall side of the culvert from the, as yet, unused pipes. The acting trustee of the property had therefore refused his sanction to the widening of the highway down to Knutsford-road until the obooxious smell has been stopped. This was the reason why the work had been delayed, and they considered they were justified in so acting until they were satisfied that the poisonous gases should not be conveyed from Thelwall township into the Grappenhall district. At Dr Adams' suggestion the mouth of the pipe had been closed. Mr Linaker : That is carrying the war into the enemy's camp!

Tho- Clerk also read a letter from F Leah, High Legh, who wrots under date 7th September complaining that the stench had been emanating from the tannery all the past weak. and that the surveyor had said the stench was very bad. Writing under date September 1902 Mr Naylor said that referring to the drainage system and water supply Dr Penny had already stated that the system was satisfactory. The County Analyst had declared tne water to be hard but good while the bacteriological (report stated that the bacilla could not be regarded as an actual cause of disease. Mr Naylor then went on to trace the action of the Council in dealing with the matter and referred to the dreadful outbreaks of diphtheria which had never previously occurred prior to the horrid smells. In conclusion Mr Naylor quoted De Penny who when dealing with the tannery stated " The effluvia from such matters are unquestionably danger- ous and a fruitful source of much fatal disease."

The following telegram was sent by Mr Naylor, London, under date September 9th :--" To Chairman District Council Board Room, Dutton, Preston Brook. Respecting your Medical Officer's condemnation of water supply oc my property at Thelwall I wrote Cou oty Analyst. Please communicate his reply to your Council. 'I am verylmuch surprised to bear that any Medical officer should condemn a water which I have passed as pore.' Ido not think you !amid trouble your- self about the medical officer's remarks."

Under date August 29th, Mr Naylor wrote to the Clerk as folhave I have yours of the 27th but no reply to my last. Before asking far this through the Local Cr-mum:tent Bard, I give you the chance of replying. I notice that your officers are to make an inspection of my property but you did not send me the statutory notice, stating time of , inspection. I have waited a poet but none has arrived this morning I trust you will forward this without delay and give me sufficient notice to enable me to arrange with some London scientist to represent me on the occasion. Seeing that sour Medical Officer and In- spector flatly contradicted a statement the former made to me and this " direct traverse "was given to your Council I shall not accept any report either of these said officials may present without my being protected by a representative. The Clerk said that he had sent a cimy of the correi• pandenne to the medical officer and had asked Imo to Prepare and submit a report to the Council that day fortnight so that the Council might furnish a report to the County Council.

Dr Adams said that he had already got his report written and would read it to the Council. He would first of all like to say that the original reports asked for by Admiral Parry and Mr Naylor had been in possession of the Local Government Board. He was now furnished with copies of the reports and MrNayler could have them when he so desired. Continuing the medical officer said that!lin investigating the causes which led ta the diphtheria outbreaks be had arloptel three causes. , He first examined the tanyard. Nothing however, was discovered and there was nothing in his opinion that would lead to:the production of such a disease. He next made a bacteriological examinatinn of the two drinking waters from Mr Naylor's well and Mr Reynold 's. The samples frornlMr Naylot's which were sent to an analyst contained 5,324 organisms per cubic centimetre a number of the colon communis bacilli being found. The analyst also stated that' this sample of water has recently been contaminated and is at present unfit for drinking purposes." At the time no information was given to the analyst about the 9amplo. On asking for further informatioo the analyst sitd that the water contained bacteria of the stepti cocci group, the total number being 1,400 per cubic centimetre which far exceeded the limit of 100 per cubic centimetre. The analyst commenting ortiMr Reynolds's water said that the water contained 173 bacteria per cubic centimet re, the stepti cocci not being found in 60 cubic centimetres. Bacteriologically it was one of remarkable purity, his impression being that in its pre- sent condition it was improbable that it was serving, as a vehiole for the dissemination of diphtheria. Dr Adams commenting rn the report of the analyst, said there could be no question about Mr Naylor's water being polluted, y.hile Mr Reynolds's was quite free from con- tamination. It was on these grounds that be (Dr Adams) had condemned the water for drinking purposes, exc,pt after long boiling and subsequent filtration through a filter. Dr Adams also read a report of a master sanitary plumber engaged to examine the drains, which was to the effect that the drains required attention, and that at certain places there was nothing to prevent the sewage smell from escaping. The Council eventually decided to send a copy or the Medical Officer's report to the Local Government Board, the County Council, and Mr Naylor.

div.head: WIDNES TOWN COUNCIL. -- Discussions Upon Principles. The Mayoralty.
div.p: WIDNES TOWN COUNCIL. -- Discussions Upon Principles. The Mayoralty.

The usual monthly meeting of he Town Council Was held in the Council Chamber on Tuesday afterooon.—Nlr Councillor Laws, in moving the report of the Heath Committee, congratulated the borough upon the low death rate of last month, and upon the fact that only two cases of typhoid fever had been notified. The Park and Cemetery Committee recommended the employment of a policeman on Sunday afternoon in the Park. The Chairman of the Commilt3e. Alder:man Shuttleworth, stated that there had been some trouble with boisterous youth.. The cost would be about 59 3d for an officer from 2p m until cloging time. Alderman Neil said he objected to pay for the services of a constable when they paid a large sum annually for the policing of the town. The recommendation was adopted. When the report of the Horses and Stables Committee was submitted,the Chairman (Councillor R. Allen) stated that the committee had been unable to obtain tenders for fodder, except at exorbitant prices, and as a conse- quence the committee had entrusted him 89 chairman with the duty of supplying the fodder in small quantities until they obtained tend,rs. He had bought a load at much less cost and of bettnr quality than that for which they bad obtained tenders. Alderman Timmis said, with all due respect to the chairman of the Health C im- mittee, who was withont doubt honest and straightfor• ward, be must say that they were establishing a bad and deleterioue principle.—Onuncillor Allen: And that is thanks for driving my cob fourteen miles 6n Saturday afternoon to buy hay for you. The committee's minutes were adopted. _ _

A comMunication was received from Mr S Brilhonse, county coroner, urging the establishment of a cent*.l mortuary for the borough. sad stating that at two recent inquests the juries had made recommendations urgine the necesaity of such a building. The matter was referred to the Health Committee

At the conclusion of the Council meeting,a meeting of a more informal character wee held. at which the pre- sent Mayor (Alderman W W Gosseze) was unanimopsiy invited to accept office for a second year, and was heartily congratulated upon his successful cervices as Mayor during the Coronation year.—The Mayor pro- mised to reply at the neat meeting, and in the mean- time thanked the Council for their invitation. 30,000 restored 'their r-starielehtt LsloNr:33d 11;y"TILELBLohR7e141,adox' Manchester. div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
Increase of the Poor Rate.

A meeting of the Warrington Board of Gaardians was held in the Board Room at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. Dr Patterson presided, and there were also present :—Mrs Clay, Rev Father Wilson, Rev T R Matthews, Messrs G Pilling, J Payton, T H Ashcroft, 9 Davies, A J Jolley, J Clarke, J Bißinge, J Turton, William Houghton, G Mather, J Backhouse, R Forshaw, T Ritchie, J Robinson, A Jolley, T Halton, with J C , Sutton (clerk), 8 Sutton (assistant clerk), F Gate (master), and A Wright (superintendent Padgate Schools).

PADGATE SCHOOLS.—.PROPOSED EXTENSION. The Padgat3 Schools Committee recommended th 3 appointment of an additional assistant schoolmistress (non-resident) at an annual salary of £65. Mr A J JOLLEY, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said he would like to say a few words about the pro- posed addition to the staff, rendered necessary by the fact that the sehocle were now abselutely full. The Local Government Board School Inspector, two years ago April, sueges'ed to the Committee that the staff needed increasing. The Committee did not concur in the opinion of Mr Mozley, and up to the present had not increased the staff. He ventured to think they weuld not have increased the staff now were it not for the fact that the number of children of echo° 'age had now increased to such an extent that it was imperative to appoint an additional teacher. Ur Mozley suggested two, but the provision of one would I put the Board on the same footing as an elementary 'school in regard to its teaching staff and the committee would be justified in appointing one t. achrr. I Mr WILLIAM HOUGHTON said he had been rather puzzled to know what was the cause of the extraordin- ary increase in the number of childreo admitted to the sohoels. Fcr many year.] the number of children ad- mitted was normal but there had been a large incresee lately and the schcole were becoming overcrowded. He had found one reason tbat morning. The inerease was accountable, be thought, to the large number .3f children admitted swing to the prosecutions of the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children. The parents were sent to orison and the children were taken to the schools. During the last few years, 33 children had been admitted under such circomstances.

Mr A J JOLLEY said one or two members of the corn- mittee seemed to be of opinion that possibly the large number of children in the schools was due to a little laxity on the part of the relief committees in helping widows and families by taking two or more children to the schools and relieving distress in that form. Ho did not wish to express any opinion but he would like to suggest that it was desirable every half-rear that the three relief committees should very carefully supervise the lists for their respective districts and make sure that no unnecessary relief was given in that form. It was possible there might be one or two instances in which relief had been given unnecessarily by relieving parents of the care of their children. If the committees would instruct their officers to investi- gate the eircumstraces of each case a thorough revision could be made.
Mr Fonuseis : I don't think the outside districts send any children to the school. Mr PILLING: That is so.
Mr BILLINGE : The Board has spent's lot of money in advertising the schools by means of illustrated pamph- lets and slow we have the result.
Mr JOLLEY • Quite right too - • . •

Mr BILLINGE said he believed the Board was indebted to a member for a rural district for the suggestion re- specting the advertising of the schools. They had now to pay for the result of it. Mr A J Jom.xy said personally he did not shrink from maintaining that the policy of giving relief by taking children to Padgate Schools was a wise acid proper one and he hoped the Board would not shrink from its duty. Anxious consideration had been given to the desirability of extending the accommodation for children at Padgate schools. He did not wish to broach that subject now, but he would only say that on the previ- ous day, the Schools Committee decided to make the r next meeting of the Board a special one for the purpose of consid -ring tho desirability of inereasiag the accom- modation at Padgate. FORSHAW : Rave vol had an intimation to in- Grease the accommodation ?
Mr A J JOLLEY : No ;to increase the staff. Ttio recorninondation wag annroverl. HOUSE COMMITTEE. THE GROCERY CONTRACT.

At a meeting of the House Committee held on 29th August a letter was read from the Warrington and Dis- trict Grocer4' and Provision Dealers Association respect- ing the form of the grocery contract. The Master was instructed to reply that their request had been met by • revision ot the old contract, and that in consequence of the advertisement having been issued, they could not grant the interview asked.—at a prior meeting of the commiPtee it was regolved that the tender of Mr George Hoult for the outs;de painting of the Workhouse premises also for the inside psirVisre of no dining hall for the sum of £l6O be accepted. The Master submitted revised forms of tender for the half-yearly contracts, which the committee adoped and recommended that new samples be obtained for the guidance of contractors The' minutes were eonfirmed HALF-YEARLY CONTRACTS.

The following tenders were accepted :—Meat, Mr Singleton ; flour and meal, Messrs Carter and Son ; bread,Mr James Hallwood; milk (schools), Mr Houghton; milk kworkbouse), Farmers Stores ; straw and potatoes, expire of E Warburton ; leather, Messrs Pickavance and Son ; clogs, Mr William Jone ; drapery, cord and twill. Mr T J Lee ; brushes, Mr G Ratcliffe ; glazing, Mr R Razeldine ' • wine and spirits, Me T W Pickmere. The contracts for groceries, coal, boots and shoes, and Coffins were referred to the Rouse Committee.

Mr BILLINGE asked whether some of the calls were not owing yet ? The CLERIC : There is not as much owing as there was twelve months ago, and the balance is £2,000 lesa.

Mr FORSRAW said he asked at the time whethrr the Newton offices could be built out of a sixpenny rate and the Clerk said vrs. The CLERK : No. no. I said if you wanted it to be done by a sixpenny rate you must give me authority to borrow the money on loan. It was decided not to take up a
Mr Firtsmaw : A Int of these thins are tring paid out of current reoPnue P

The CLERK : You pay everything out of current revenpe except the loans which you have authorised. It is all the better if you can pay everything out of revenue. Ttrre are no law charges to pay and no charges for interest in connection with loans. Mr A. J. JOLLEY said he differed in some respects from the policy of what he might term th-, unnecessarily ner- vous timidity from borrowine money which might 1/4, legitimately borrowed for expenditure of a capital nature. That had undoubtedly been the policy of the Board in the past and he believed if they levied a special rate of ls 61 in the 2, it woull pay off all the loans outstanding at the present time. (Rear, hear ) A union that had only cot a debt on capital account of that amount was in a position to be congratulated, 14ut be thought a bolder policy in the past would have bri.r: wiser, and he holy,d a bolder policy would be adoptc.d in the future. It was a fact that the work of the Union had been hampered by:what he had described as nervous hesitation in facing their financial obligations. In Corroboration o his statement, Mr Jolley proceeded to read the Clerk's report of la months ago, which he 8,03 reflected most seriously on the past policy of the Board. For many a year in successive years some of the more pressing needs of the Union were deferred for monetary reasons, and he contended that in cansequonce unneces- sary suffering was inflicted on the poor. He objected to such * policy and should always vote against it. What- I ever they did they ought to face their responsibilities in ; an intelligent way and give the best possible treatment they could to the children in the schools and to the I

deserving and aged poor, whilst at the same time being as stria as they possibly could in dealing with appli- cants of a less satisfactory character in granting relief, and in dealing with people who ought to maintain tnesn- selves outside. Do not let them shirk their duty, and, if necessary, as on this occasion, making an appeal to the ratepayers when more money Was needed. Ile did not cast any reflection on the Newton Committee in providing new offices. Such offices ought to have been provided long ago. He objected to the attempt to pay for the offices out of revenue, they might have paid for them out of a loan and kept within a sixpenny rate. Within the last five years the Union had paid from £7,000 to £B,OOO out of revenue, which might have been raised by a 10210. That means you have been paying a penny in the £ more than you need. Mr ASHCROFT : Our friend Mr J olley is coming out next November. (Laughter.) The CLERK said he should think the Board had paid £20,000 out of revenue that most unions would have borrowed. If the Board had not done that they would not have been in the position that Mr Jolley congratu- ated them upon, namely that a rate of is 6d in the £ would clear the Union of all its loans. They could not have reduced the poor rate from is in the £ in winter and 10.1 in rho £ in summer to a uniform rate of six- pence in the £ if the Board had borrowed that £20,000 instead of paying it out of revenue. He would like Mr Jolley to read an article in the " Times " upon the course taken by the English railway companies as regards the borrowing of capital. If Mr Jolley would read it carefully he would find a good deal of ground for the course he (the Clerk) had taken. In referring to the delay in carrying out reforms, the Clerk said the poor had not suffered by it. The inmates were kindly treated, but the accommodation was not up to the most recent requirements. They could not build schools and infirmaries all at once. Toe Board was obliged to have time.

The following resolution was then passed :—" That the estimates of expenditure for the half year ending at Lady Day, 1903, be approved, and that the Clerk be instructed to prepare contribution orders upon the several townships in accordance therewith. After con- clusion of revision of valuation lists and supplemental lists and approval thereof by the Assessment Commit- tee."

div.head: REGISTRATION ARRANGEMENTS AT SANKEY, PENKETH AND BURTONWOOD.
div.p: REGISTRATION ARRANGEMENTS AT SANKEY, PENKETH AND BURTONWOOD.

Mt Joseph Smith was'called into the room with refer- , ence to his appointment to the offices of registrar of births and deaths and vaccination officer for the districts of Great Sankey, Peaketh, Cuerdley and Burtonwood, and for consideration of his residence: and registration arrangements. In answer to the Chairman. Mr SMITH said he was willing to carry out any arrangements the Board might ' suggest with reterence to his residence. After some discussion, it was decided on the proposi- tion of Mr HALTON, that Mr Smith be allowed ro reside , at his present residence in Liverpool-road, Great Sankey, I on condition that he bad a place of call at Burtonwood, where be would attend twice weekly for 1.1 hours each visit (say on Tuesday morning and Friday evening) and also a place of call near the Ponketh Post Office. where he would attend for an hour on Wednesday in each week for the convenience of Penketh and Cuerdley residents. An amendment proposed by Mr FORSHAW, that a com- mittee be appointed to define the position where Mr Smith should live, was lost. . _ . _ .
Mr BACKHOUSE remark,d that Mr Forehaw wa3 like the bov who cried for the moon. (Lmghter.) He wanted what he could not get. Mr Foasnew : Solomon on the prophet. (Laughter.)

The judges I were : Messrs S Thomason and 0 Marsh for 'vege- tables; Messrs Clare and Parker for flowers, plants, &c.• ; Mrs Withington, Culcheth Hall, and Mrs Williams, Orford, for children's wild flowers. The two latter awarded the prizes to the children as follows :—Seniors; I, C Callaghan ; 2, W Callaghan; 13, 0 Sankey ; 4, S Sankey. Juniors: 1, Annie Dodd; 2, S Sybil Cawthorn's ; 3, A Cawthorne ; 4, Gertie Cooper. Miss Comber, of Middleton Hall, kindly gave consolation prizes to the unsuccessful emu- ' petitots. The Sports Committee had arranged for I athletic sports, which were held in a field kindly placed at their disposal by Mr L. Birchall. div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.
Benefit Concert in the Co-operative Hall.

A grand benefit concert (arranged by Miss E Plinston and Mr W Shaw) was held in the Co-oper- ative Hall, Sankey-street, on Monday evening,in aid of Henry Woolley, cabman, who has had his foot amputated. There was a large audience,Mr James Dodds occupying the chair.—Theprogramme opened with a song, " Mona," by Mr Arthur Griffiths,whose sweet tenor voice was helrd to great advantage in I the rendering of that piece, and the audience show- ed their appreciation by loudly applauding him. Madame F Christiau Wild heard to advantage In "The promise of life." A violin solo was also given with marked ability by Mr S Rowland. Mr E Pearce, LRC M, who possesses a rich bass voice, delighted the audience with "Father O'Flynn," and he gave as an encore " Queen of the earth," which was equally pleasing. An appreciable solo, "Enchantress,' was painstakingly rendered by Miss Nellie Anderton, the company' insisting upon her re-appearance, and in a fine contralto voiee she gave "The sweetest flower that blooms." The lEolian glee singers—Messrs H Bennett (alto), W White (first tenor), W nnett (second tenor), and W Knowles (bass)—earned the applause of the assembly in" Of a' the airts the wind can blow," and gave in response to their continued applause that amusing piece, "He that hath a pleasent face." Much ability was shown in a 'cello' solo by Mr E Balmferd. Messrs. A Griffiths and E H Pearce gave the duet, " Love and war," which was greatly enjoyed, and elicited an encore. After an interval of five minutes, Mr Arthur Griffiths led the second part of the programme with " Mary of Argyle," gaining hearty rounds of applause. Madame F. Christian's soprano voice gave a clear expression to the song, " Come, sweet morning," and sh 3 gave as an encore, " Would you ?" The audience greatly appreciated the solo. "The heart bowed down," by 'Mr E A Pearce, elicited an encore, and he responded with "Storm Fiend." Mr S Rowland contributed a violin solo in an able manner, proving with each stroke of the bow his high accomplishments. Miss Anderton again pleased the audience with " Good bye.' giving Within your heart" in response to ' the hearty applause of the company, The Aolian glee singers were heard to advantage in "Frank- lin's Deg..' Their encore "Robin Adair" was equally appreciated. A 'cello solo was given with much precision by Mr E Balmford, Mr Albert E Trow was an excellent accompanist. Too much praise cannot be given to Mr E Sanders for the fascinating elocution with which he entertained the audience as humorist Mr J J Moreton moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman' artistes, and Miss Plinston and Mr Shaw, and this was seconded by Mr T Trow.—The Chairman suit- ably responded,and a pleasant evening was brought to a close by singing the first verse of the National , Anthem. ASH for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-OL ASS MINERAL wATHILS.—Advt. The Weaver Navigation Trustees and the Late Mr E. Milner.

At a meeting of the Weaver Navigation Trustees, held on Monday, at Northwich, the Chairman (Colonel France-Hayhurst), said: Before we com- mence business I should like to allude to the great loss that all we on this Trust have sustained by the death of our old friend, Mr Edward Milner, who was quiet and unostentatious he manner, and was singularly clear-headed, and of great business capacity. Whatever he did, he did thoroughly, and well He will be greatly missed particularly by this Trust,and also by the other hoards and authori- ties which be represented. He was a personal friend of my own, and I beg to move "That the Weaver Navigation Trustees desire to express the profound sorrow felt by them at the lamented death of Mr Edward Milner, vice-chairman of the Trust, and of the Finance and Works Committee, and to record their sense of the serious loss to the Trust thereby of one who by the able business capacity, impartiality, and sound common sense which he brought to bear on all matters con- nected with the interests of the Trust proved him- self to be One of its most valued members; and they offer their sincere sympathy and condolence with Mrs Milner and family :n their bereavement "—Mr Ward : I rise to second the resolution which hes been placed before us. It is not necessary for me to say many words, for I think almost everything has been said. Mr Milner himself was not a man of many words. I speak of him, hAving met him in connection with many other companies and busi- nesses, and there was no man with whom it was more pleasant to do businees. It is a very great loss to us, and I know of no man in whom you could place more confidence. He was honest, and everyone felt that they were dealing with a per- sonal friend. I myself have worked with 'him for many years' and I feel it a personal logs, and I feel sure that the whole of the traders will also feel the same. (Hear, hear.) I beg to second it,—Canon Armistead supported the resolution which was carried. PUBLIC MINTIFIT UNDER 2114110LOOKIFon BUST BOOTS IN LANCIA SHIM—Mot

div.head: WIRRAL AND BIRKENHEAD SHOW.
div.p: WIRRAL AND BIRKENHEAD SHOW.
A Record Entry.

W rra and tiirlzonhoad agrnanteuraltioefel7.wh':'`' this year nel,braona Its Dianannd Jublipp, opened its annual two-days' snow on Wednesday at 'tebington,with every prospect of scoring another pronounced success. True, the climatic conditions in the early morning wore anything but nromiding, and a slight rain shower of short duration caused the promoters of the show a con- siderable amount of anxiety. In the course of the forenooo a strong, cutting brec ze sprang up, rendering the conditions under which the large attendance of vis'tors viewed the exhibits anything but pleas" set, The Coutcil, along with the secretary, Mr Arthur H Ed wardson, had made every preparation in the splendidly-equipped grounds With for the live stock and thnse who came to see them, and a word of praise is certainly due to that bGly of gentle- So far as entries en a record was easily constitu- ted, the figures being 6.203, as against 3,328 in 1900 and 6,160 in 1899. The number was reached mainly by the aid of pigeons (1,596), dogs (1,140), and horticulture (1,162), though in horses, sheep, and ,cattle the figures had gone up considerably, and it is, perhaps, worthy of note that the entries work out at nearly six times as many as there were at the Cheshire show held at Hyde the other Saturday. In the open classes were included some of the bnst known exhibitors in the United King- dom, amongst them being several who carried off high honours at the Royal Lancashire Show at Preston last week. The attractive nature of the ptivi list, which oontains no fewer than four 50-guinea cups and the Macgregor Laird Commemoration Bowl valued at 100 guineas, was, no doubt, responsible for large entries of horses, regarded both in the matter of number and quality, as the best seen in the show-yard during the long history of the society. The cattle too, were of a uniformly first-rate character, whilst some of the best dogs in the country were benched. The horticultural section was far ahead of those of previous years. A. great crowd of specta,ors wituess2d the leaping in the afternoon, when some capital horsemanship was seen.

Alt work to be completed before 8 o'6lock in the morning Of each day, and privies and ashpits. and all places where tlightsoll has been deposited, to be treated with carbolic or Other disinfecting powder to be supplied by the Council to the Contractor. This having been an exceptionally wet summer, dresses of heavy material, such as serge or tweed, have had an unusual amount of hard wear, while the dainty muslins,. linens and piques have perforce been neglected, except during the all too brief period of sunshine when we have found relief in their fresh beauty. Those who at the commencement of the summer season were wise enough to invest in a good, well-fitting coat and skirt costume will by now have reaped the benefit of their sensible selection. There is certainly no sign of any waning in popularity of this useful and economical style of out-door dress, which finds favour in the eyes of the highest and the humblest woman in the land by reason of its exceeding good qualities. Both indoors and out the skirt, if plain and well fitting, can be worn with a pretty blouse, while for cold days a smart Little coat is invaluable. There are many very neatly made coats and skirts to be bought ready- made, but these, although• they look very well, cannot stand so much hard wear as when one purchases the material and has it made to order. Too much expense is wasted on the trimming of these ready-made garments, the material naturally suffering and being of inferior quality. If one can afford a frequent change of dress there is no doubt that a ready-made gown is a great convenience, especially to those of an ordinary middle height, say five feet four or five inches, but for anyone who is unusually tall or short or particularly stout, a specially cut and fitted costume is required. A neat autumn costume is sketched, made of reddish brown frieze trimmed with a little braid to match. The coat can be worn open or closed as desired, a great convenience in this country of ours where the weather changes so

The Blackbrook Store belonging to the St. Helens Co-operative Society, was entered during Friday night or Saturday morning, and £164 taken from the safe. The thieves are supposed to have entered by the front door, and secured a key of the safe. The premises were locked up about a quarter past ten on Friday night by the manager, and when he went at eight o'clock on Saturday morning he found that the back door was open. From the conditien of the premises it is thought that the thieves opened the front door in the ordinary way with a key, and went right througo the place,keep- ing the back door open as a means of escape. The safe was behind the counter, close to the front door, and this had been opened and completely cleared. Constable Thomas was immediately called and he and Sergeant Walker and the Cooperative officials are investigating the matter.

ENDING AUGUST 30TH, 1902. During the week the following births and deaths, were registered : Warrington registration district : births, 49 ; deaths 17. The excess of births over deaths was 32. The birth-rate was equal to 388. The death-rate from all causes was equal to 13 4 per 1,000 against 12-4 the average of the previous 4 weeks, and against 16.1 the corresponding period of last year. Tbe death-rate from the seven chief zymotic diseases was equal to 15 per 1,000, against '7 the average rate of the previous 4 weeks, and against 6.4 the corres- ponding period of 1901. The ages of mortality were:- 0-1 1-5 5-15 15-25 25-65 65 up. Total. 6 1 1 6 3 17 The deaths included :—Diarrhcea, 1; whooping cough 1 ; lung diseases, 2; heart diseases, 3; injuries, 2 ; al other causes, 8. The following cases of infectious disease have been reported during this week :—Scarlet fever, 5. Total number of patients in hospital week ending August 30th, 33. METEOROLOGY.—The mean temperature was 52. Fah., and therefore the same as the preceding week. The maximum temperature 72 F., was recorded on the 28th August, and the minimum temperature 43 F. on the 26th August. The rainfall measured 'O3 inch. The general direc- tion was S.E. J. WARRINGTON. The Tramways. About 50 men in the service of the London and North-Western Railway Company wer3 engaged during the greater part of Sunday in putting down the rails at Wilderspool Crossing. The work was carried out under the direction of Mr Turnbull (assistant to Mr Andrews, of the Permanent Way Department), the Borough Surveyor being also present on behalf of the Corporation. Work in close proximity to the crossing has yet to be done. but it is expected that the tramway service to Stockton Reath will be opened in about three weeks.
